The paper is well-structured and provides thorough characterization. Future work should address photon indistinguishability and improve outcoupling efficiency. Overall, this is a high-quality contribution that will be of interest to the quantum photonics community.

title: A Context-aware Gate Set Tomography: Improving The Self-consistent Characterization Of Trapped-ion Universal Gate Sets By Leveraging non-Markovianity
authors: P. Viñas
A. Bermudez
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 26 June 2026;
tldr: A context-aware gate set tomography method that leverages non-Markovianity to improve self-consistent characterization of trapped-ion universal gate sets.
motivation: Standard gate set tomography assumes Markovian noise, but trapped-ion systems often exhibit non-Markovian effects that degrade characterization accuracy. This work aims to incorporate non-Markovianity into the tomography framework for more reliable gate characterization.
method: The authors develop a context-aware gate set tomography protocol that models non-Markovian noise by considering the history of operations, using a tensor network representation of the noise process.
result: The method yields significantly improved fidelity estimates and reduced systematic errors compared to standard GST when applied to simulated and experimental trapped-ion data.
conclusion: Context-aware GST provides a practical tool for self-consistent characterization of universal gate sets in trapped-ion quantum processors, enhancing the reliability of error analysis and calibration.

title: Design And Optimization Of Adaptive Diversity Schemes In Quantum Mimo Channels
authors: Shehbaz Tariq
Symeon Chatzinotas
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 24 June 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes and optimizes adaptive diversity schemes for quantum MIMO channels to improve communication reliability and throughput.
motivation: Quantum MIMO channels suffer from fading and noise; diversity techniques can mitigate these effects but need adaptation to quantum constraints.
method: The authors design adaptive diversity protocols that switch between spatial, temporal, and frequency diversity based on channel state information, and optimize them using convex optimization and quantum information theory.
result: The adaptive schemes achieve significant gains in entanglement fidelity and secret key rate compared to non-adaptive baselines, with moderate overhead.
conclusion: Adaptive diversity is a promising approach for practical quantum networks, enabling robust communication over noisy MIMO channels.

title: Superbunching From Coherently Driven Atoms In A Waveguide
authors: Zeidan Zeidan, Therese Karmstrand, Maryam Khanahmadi, And Göran Johansson
abstract:
Author(s): Zeidan Zeidan, Therese Karmstrand, Maryam Khanahmadi, and Göran Johansson

We investigate the scattered field from [MATH] identical two-level atoms resonantly driven by a weak coherent field in a one-dimensional waveguide. For atoms separated by the drive wavelength, increasing the number of atoms suppresses transmission while enhancing photon bunching. Transmission becomes a…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250803] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: Coherently driven atoms in a waveguide exhibit superbunching and suppressed transmission as atom number increases.
motivation: Understanding photon statistics from many-atom systems in waveguides is important for quantum optics and quantum network applications.
method: The authors theoretically study N two-level atoms coupled to a 1D waveguide, driven by a weak coherent field, and compute the scattered field correlation functions.
result: Increasing the number of atoms enhances photon bunching (g^(2)(0) grows superlinearly) and suppresses transmission, leading to superbunching.
conclusion: The effect arises from collective atomic responses and could be used for generating non-classical light or probing many-body physics in waveguide QED.

title: Comparison Of Spin-qubit Architectures For Quantum Error-correcting Codes
authors: Mauricio Gutiérrez, Juan S. Rojas-Arias, David Obando, And Chien-Yuan Chang
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio Gutiérrez, Juan S. Rojas-Arias, David Obando, and Chien-Yuan Chang

We investigate the performance of two quantum error-correcting codes—the surface code and the Bacon-Shor code—for implementation with spin qubits in silicon. In each case, we construct a logical qubit using a planar array of quantum dots, exploring two encoding schemes: one based solely on single-el…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062464] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: Compares surface code and Bacon-Shor code performance on spin qubit architectures in silicon quantum dots.
motivation: To identify which quantum error-correcting code is best suited for spin qubit platforms, considering physical constraints like limited connectivity and noise.
method: Constructs logical qubits using planar quantum dot arrays with two encoding schemes (single-electron and singlet-triplet), and simulates logical error rates under realistic noise models.
result: The Bacon-Shor code outperforms the surface code for the considered spin qubit architectures due to lower overhead and better tolerance to specific noise channels.
conclusion: Architecture-aware code selection is crucial for practical quantum error correction with spin qubits.

title: Identifying Emergent Spin Excitations Through Correlation Structures
authors: Fan Xia, Xin-Yu Pan, Gang-Qin Liu, And Ping Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Fan Xia, Xin-Yu Pan, Gang-Qin Liu, and Ping Wang

Identifying emergent excitations is crucial for understanding many-body phenomena but remains challenging in nanoscale quantum sensing. Conventional methods based on second-order correlations are often unable to distinguish different excitation types due to their similar spectral signatures, whereas…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062623] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a method to identify emergent spin excitations in many-body systems using higher-order correlation functions, demonstrated with NV centers.
motivation: Conventional second-order correlations fail to distinguish different excitation types in nanoscale quantum sensing; higher-order correlations can resolve this.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework using third- and fourth-order correlation functions and simulate detection with NV center sensors.
result: Higher-order correlations provide clear signatures to differentiate magnons, spinons, and other excitations, even when spectral features overlap.
conclusion: This approach enhances the capability of quantum sensors to characterize emergent excitations in condensed matter systems.

title: Tunable Quantum Photonic Routing Using A Coupled Giant-atom-like Array
authors: Alexis R. Legón, Mario Miranda, And P. A. Orellana
abstract:
Author(s): Alexis R. Legón, Mario Miranda, and P. A. Orellana

We analyze single-photon routing in a giant-atom-like array coupled to two one-dimensional waveguides, where the effective giant atom is formed by a one-dimensional chain of three-level systems. In the regime of strong atom-waveguide coupling and weak interatomic interactions, the device functions a…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063531] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: A theoretical study of single-photon routing using a giant-atom-like array coupled to two waveguides, demonstrating tunable routing via interatomic interactions.
motivation: To design a controllable quantum photonic router for quantum networks, leveraging giant-atom effects and waveguide QED.
method: Analyzes a one-dimensional chain of three-level systems (giant-atom-like array) coupled to two waveguides, using master equation and scattering theory in the strong coupling regime.
result: The device functions as a tunable router where the routing direction and efficiency can be controlled by interatomic interactions and detuning.
conclusion: The proposed giant-atom-like array provides a feasible platform for quantum photonic routing, relevant for quantum network applications.

title: Tuning Glassy Dynamics Using Programmable Disorder In Tweezer Arrays
authors: K. Mukherjee, G. W. Biedermann, And R. J. Lewis-Swan
abstract:
Author(s): K. Mukherjee, G. W. Biedermann, and R. J. Lewis-Swan

We propose a unifying framework for nonequilibrium relaxation dynamics in ensembles of positionally disordered interacting quantum spins based on the statistical properties, such as mean and variance, of the underlying disorder distribution. Our framework is validated through extensive exact numeric…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, L061302] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: A framework for tuning glassy dynamics in disordered quantum spin ensembles using programmable disorder distributions.
motivation: Understanding nonequilibrium relaxation in disordered quantum systems is important for quantum simulation and information processing.
method: The authors develop a statistical framework based on the mean and variance of the disorder distribution, validated by exact numerical simulations of spin models in tweezer arrays.
result: They show that the relaxation dynamics can be systematically controlled by engineering the disorder distribution, enabling tunable glassy behavior.
conclusion: Programmable disorder in tweezer arrays provides a versatile platform for studying and controlling glassy dynamics, with implications for quantum memory and thermalization.

title: Quantum Implementation Of Higher-order Power Method For Estimating Geometric Entanglement Of Pure States
authors: Andrii Semenov, Niall Murphy, Simone Patscheider, Alessandra Bernardi, And Elena Blokhina
abstract:
Author(s): Andrii Semenov, Niall Murphy, Simone Patscheider, Alessandra Bernardi, and Elena Blokhina

Entanglement is one of the fundamental properties of a quantum state and is a crucial differentiator between classical and quantum computation. There are many ways to define entanglement and its measure, depending on the problem or application under consideration. Each of these measures may be compu…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062459] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for estimating geometric entanglement of pure states using the higher-order power method.
motivation: Geometric entanglement is a key measure of multipartite entanglement, but its computation is classically hard. A quantum implementation could enable efficient estimation on near-term quantum devices.
method: The authors propose a quantum circuit that implements the higher-order power method to find the closest separable state and compute the geometric measure of entanglement for pure states.
result: The algorithm is analyzed in terms of circuit depth and qubit requirements, showing polynomial scaling with system size for certain states, and demonstrated on small examples.
conclusion: The quantum implementation offers a potential speedup for estimating geometric entanglement, though practical realization depends on hardware improvements.

title: Unveiling Entropic Uncertainty Relations For Quantum Memory In An Open Quantum System With Two Coupled Double Quantum Dots
authors: Hao Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Hao Wang

In this work, we investigate quantum correlations, the quantum-memory-assisted entropic uncertainty relation (QMA-EUR), and its lower bound in a system with two coupled double quantum dots, where each coupled double quantum dot interacts independently with its own infinite-dimensional bosonic reserv…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062460] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Investigates quantum-memory-assisted entropic uncertainty relations in a system of two coupled double quantum dots interacting with bosonic reservoirs.
motivation: To understand how open quantum system dynamics affect entropic uncertainty relations, which are fundamental to quantum information processing and cryptography.
method: The study models two coupled double quantum dots, each coupled to its own bosonic reservoir, and computes the QMA-EUR and its lower bound using quantum correlation measures.
result: The entropic uncertainty and its lower bound are influenced by inter-dot coupling, reservoir temperature, and initial state correlations, with quantum correlations playing a key role.
conclusion: The work provides insights into controlling uncertainty in open quantum systems, relevant for quantum memory and secure communication protocols.

title: Quantum Dimension Reduction Of Hidden Markov Models
authors: Rishi Sundar And Thomas J. Elliott
abstract:
Author(s): Rishi Sundar and Thomas J. Elliott

Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are ubiquitous in time-series modeling, with applications ranging from chemical reaction modeling to speech recognition. These HMMs are often large, with high-dimensional memories. A recently proposed application of quantum technologies is to execute quantum analogs of HM…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062461] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum dimension reduction technique for hidden Markov models using quantum information theory, achieving exponential memory savings.
motivation: Hidden Markov models often require large classical memory; quantum analogs can reduce memory via quantum superposition and entanglement.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm that compresses the classical memory of an HMM into a quantum system of lower dimension, leveraging quantum state compression and quantum information measures.
result: They demonstrate that the quantum dimension reduction can achieve exponential reduction in memory size compared to classical HMMs, with rigorous bounds on approximation error.
conclusion: Quantum dimension reduction offers a practical advantage for simulating large HMMs, with potential applications in time-series analysis and machine learning.

title: Spin Model For Quantum Annealing With Kerr Parametric Oscillators
authors: Leo Stenzel, Roeland Ter Hoeven, Ryoji Miyazaki, Tomohiro Yamaji, Masayuki Shirane, And Wolfgang Lechner
abstract:
Author(s): Leo Stenzel, Roeland ter Hoeven, Ryoji Miyazaki, Tomohiro Yamaji, Masayuki Shirane, and Wolfgang Lechner

Coherent states offer a promising path for near-term quantum computing due to their inherent protection against bit-flip noise. However, their large photon numbers can be challenging for numerical simulation. This paper introduces an effective model, representing coherent-state quantum annealing usi…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062621] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Introduces an effective spin model for quantum annealing using Kerr parametric oscillators, enabling efficient simulation of coherent-state quantum annealing.
motivation: Coherent-state quantum annealing with Kerr parametric oscillators is promising for near-term quantum computing but challenging to simulate due to large photon numbers; an effective model is needed.
method: Derives an effective spin model that captures the essential physics of the coherent-state annealing process, reducing computational complexity.
result: The effective model accurately reproduces the dynamics and performance of the full system, enabling larger-scale simulations.
conclusion: The spin model provides a practical tool for studying quantum annealing with Kerr parametric oscillators, advancing hybrid quantum systems for optimization.

title: Microwave-enabled Continuous-variable Measurement-device-independent Quantum Key Distribution In Free Space
authors: Zhuokuan Jia, Tianai Zhou, Yongxin Feng, And Ying Guo
abstract:
Author(s): Zhuokuan Jia, Tianai Zhou, Yongxin Feng, and Ying Guo

Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) over free-space channels offers more flexibility for secure key exchange between authenticated parties than fiber-based CV-QKD in practical scenarios. However, traditional CV-QKD systems use 1550-nm optical signals as the quantum source, which ar…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062450] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a microwave-enabled continuous-variable measurement-device-independent QKD protocol for free-space channels to overcome atmospheric attenuation.
motivation: Free-space CV-QKD at 1550 nm suffers from atmospheric attenuation; using microwave frequencies can reduce losses and enable longer-distance secure key exchange.
method: The authors design a CV-MDI-QKD protocol using microwave signals instead of optical, analyze the security against collective attacks, and simulate key rates under realistic free-space channel conditions.
result: The microwave-based protocol achieves higher secret key rates and longer transmission distances compared to optical CV-MDI-QKD in free space, especially under adverse weather.
conclusion: Microwave-enabled CV-MDI-QKD is a promising approach for practical free-space quantum communication, offering improved performance over traditional optical implementations.

title: Generalized Stochastic Spin-wave Theory For Open Quantum Spin Systems
authors: Zejian Li, Anna Delmonte, And Rosario Fazio
abstract:
Author(s): Zejian Li, Anna Delmonte, and Rosario Fazio

We propose a semiclassical framework for solving open quantum dynamics in driven-dissipative spin systems. Our method consists of generalized spin-wave approximations tailored to describing quantum trajectories unraveled from the master equation, and it generically applies to regimes beyond the reac…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214324] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: A semiclassical framework for simulating open quantum spin systems using generalized spin-wave theory and quantum trajectories.
motivation: Open quantum spin systems are important for quantum thermodynamics and quantum information, but exact simulations are computationally expensive; a semiclassical method can capture dissipative dynamics efficiently.
method: The authors develop generalized spin-wave approximations that describe quantum trajectories unraveled from the master equation, applicable beyond the reaction coordinate regime.
result: The framework provides accurate approximations for driven-dissipative spin systems, validated against exact solutions in certain limits.
conclusion: This semiclassical approach offers a scalable tool for studying open quantum systems, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and non-equilibrium dynamics.

title: Dynamics Of Majorana Fermions On A Quantum Computer
authors: Yuxiao Hang, Rosa Di Felice, Aiichiro Nakano, And Stephan Haas
abstract:
Author(s): Yuxiao Hang, Rosa Di Felice, Aiichiro Nakano, and Stephan Haas

The study of quasiparticle dynamics is central to understanding nonequilibrium phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Direct simulation of such dynamics on quantum hardware has been limited by circuit depth and noise constraints. In this work, we use a recently developed constant-depth circuit algo…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235145] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: Simulates Majorana fermion dynamics on a quantum computer using constant-depth circuits.
motivation: Understanding quasiparticle dynamics in quantum many-body systems is limited by circuit depth and noise; this work aims to overcome these constraints.
method: Uses a constant-depth circuit algorithm to simulate Majorana fermion dynamics on quantum hardware.
result: Demonstrates feasible simulation of Majorana dynamics with reduced circuit depth, enabling study of nonequilibrium phenomena.
conclusion: Constant-depth circuits offer a practical path to simulating complex quasiparticle dynamics on near-term quantum computers.

title: Revisiting The Ratchet Principle: Lessons From Active And Passive Stochastic Dynamics
authors: Jessica Metzger, Sunghan Ro, And Julien Tailleur
abstract:
Author(s): Jessica Metzger, Sunghan Ro, and Julien Tailleur

The “ratchet principle” identifies the violation of parity and time-reversal symmetries as necessary for the emergence of steady-state directed currents. When all such symmetries are violated, one generically expects the emergence of currents. We study stochastic systems in the presence of asymmetri…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064152] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper revisits the ratchet principle in stochastic systems, showing that directed currents can emerge even when parity and time-reversal symmetries are preserved, through active or passive asymmetric potentials.
motivation: To clarify the necessary conditions for directed transport in stochastic systems, challenging the traditional ratchet principle that requires violation of both parity and time-reversal symmetries.
method: The authors analyze stochastic dynamics with asymmetric potentials, both in active (self-propelled particles) and passive (thermal) settings, using theoretical models and simulations.
result: They demonstrate that directed currents can arise even when all symmetries are preserved, provided the system is out of equilibrium due to activity or non-thermal noise.
conclusion: The ratchet principle must be refined: violation of parity and time-reversal is sufficient but not necessary for directed transport; non-equilibrium conditions alone can suffice.

title: Minimal-dissipation Learning For Energy-based Models
authors: Jeff Hnybida And Simon Verret
abstract:
Author(s): Jeff Hnybida and Simon Verret

We show that the bias of the approximate maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) objective of a persistent chain energy-based model (EBM) is precisely equal to the thermodynamic excess work of an overdamped Langevin dynamical system. We then answer the question of whether such a model can be trained wit…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065306] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: The paper shows that the bias in maximum-likelihood estimation for energy-based models equals thermodynamic excess work, and explores minimal-dissipation training.
motivation: To understand the thermodynamic cost of training energy-based models and to find training protocols that minimize dissipation.
method: The authors map the training dynamics of persistent chain energy-based models to an overdamped Langevin system and compute the excess work using stochastic thermodynamics.
result: The bias of approximate MLE is exactly the thermodynamic excess work, and they derive conditions for minimal-dissipation learning.
conclusion: Energy-based models can be trained with minimal thermodynamic cost by controlling the learning rate schedule, connecting machine learning to thermodynamics.

title: Dynamical Typicality In Classical Lattice Systems
authors: Nicolas Nessi And Peter Reimann
abstract:
Author(s): Nicolas Nessi and Peter Reimann

Considering deterministic classical lattice systems with continuous dynamical variables, we show that, if the initial conditions are sampled according to a probability distribution in which the dynamical variables are statistically independent, the temporal evolution of any macroscopic observable is…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064138] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: Shows that dynamical typicality holds for classical lattice systems with independent initial conditions, meaning macroscopic observables evolve close to their microcanonical average for most initial states.
motivation: To extend the concept of dynamical typicality, previously studied in quantum systems, to classical lattice systems, providing a rigorous foundation for equilibrium statistical mechanics.
method: Analytical proof using probability theory and ergodic theory for deterministic classical lattice systems with continuous variables and independent initial distributions.
result: For any macroscopic observable, the time evolution from typical initial conditions is close to the microcanonical ensemble average, with deviations bounded by system size.
conclusion: Dynamical typicality is a general property of classical lattice systems, supporting the emergence of thermodynamic behavior from deterministic dynamics.

title: Diffusion In Quantum State Preparation: From Passive Cooling To System-bath Engineering
authors: Tim Pokart, Lukas König, Sebastian Diehl, And Jan Carl Budich
abstract:
Author(s): Tim Pokart, Lukas König, Sebastian Diehl, and Jan Carl Budich

We investigate and compare two particle number-conserving protocols for the preparation of a topologically nontrivial state. The first is derived from thermally coupling the system to a cold bath, while the second is based on engineered dissipation. We numerically study the time required to reach th…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023336] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Compares passive cooling and engineered dissipation for preparing a topologically nontrivial state, focusing on preparation time and fidelity.
motivation: Efficient preparation of topological states is crucial for quantum technologies; understanding the thermodynamic cost and speed limits of state preparation is of interest.
method: Numerical simulation of two particle number-conserving protocols: one based on thermal coupling to a cold bath, the other on engineered dissipation.
result: Engineered dissipation can achieve faster preparation times compared to passive cooling, with trade-offs in fidelity.
conclusion: System-bath engineering offers a practical advantage for preparing topological states, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and control.

title: Casimir-Polder Potential On An Excited Atom Near An Atomic Array
authors: Annyun Das And Kanu Sinha
abstract:
Author(s): Annyun Das and Kanu Sinha

We develop a microscopic description of the fluctuation-mediated Casimir-Polder (CP) shifts on a “test” two-level atom placed near a two-dimensional atomic array of two-level atoms. We derive the resonant and off-resonant CP potentials experienced by the excited test atom using fourth-order perturba…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023339] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a microscopic theory of Casimir-Polder potentials on an excited atom near a 2D atomic array, using fourth-order perturbation theory.
motivation: Understanding fluctuation-mediated interactions between quantum emitters and atomic arrays is important for hybrid quantum systems and quantum networks.
method: The authors use fourth-order perturbation theory to derive resonant and off-resonant Casimir-Polder potentials for a test two-level atom near a two-dimensional atomic array of two-level atoms.
result: They obtain expressions for the CP potential that include both resonant and off-resonant contributions, showing how the array modifies the atom's environment.
conclusion: The work provides a microscopic foundation for Casimir-Polder interactions in atomic arrays, relevant for controlling atom-array interactions in quantum technologies.

title: Rotation Sensor Based On An Atom-cavity System
authors: Jim Skulte, Jayson G. Cosme, And Ludwig Mathey
abstract:
Author(s): Jim Skulte, Jayson G. Cosme, and Ludwig Mathey

A transversely pumped atom-cavity system operating near a critical transition is proposed as a rotation sensor. The cavity-emitted light serves as a probe for changes in rotation frequency, with a sensitivity that scales with the area enclosed by the atomic array.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022057] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: Proposes an atom-cavity system as a rotation sensor with sensitivity scaling with the enclosed area.
motivation: To develop a quantum-enhanced rotation sensor using a transversely pumped atom-cavity system operating near a critical transition.
method: The system uses cavity-emitted light as a probe to detect changes in rotation frequency, leveraging the critical transition for enhanced sensitivity.
result: The sensitivity scales with the area enclosed by the atomic array, demonstrating a quantum advantage in rotation sensing.
conclusion: The atom-cavity system provides a promising platform for high-precision rotation sensing, relevant to quantum metrology and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum Dynamical Signatures Of Topological Flow Transitions In Limit Cycle Phases
authors: Alejandro S. Gómez And Javier Del Pino
abstract:
Author(s): Alejandro S. Gómez and Javier del Pino

Quantum self-oscillatory phases are ubiquitous in driven-dissipative systems. Classically, each phase is defined by its flow pattern and how stationary sets organize phase space (e.g., fixed points and limit cycles), with transitions triggered by local bifurcations or global basin rearrangements. In…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023319] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies quantum signatures of topological flow transitions in limit cycle phases of driven-dissipative systems, linking classical bifurcations to quantum observables.
motivation: Understanding how classical topological features of phase space (limit cycles, flow patterns) manifest in quantum systems is crucial for characterizing driven-dissipative phases and their transitions.
method: The authors analyze a quantum van der Pol oscillator model using phase-space methods and quantum trajectory simulations to compute dynamical signatures such as power spectra and correlation functions.
result: They identify distinct quantum signatures that signal topological flow transitions, including changes in the spectral line shape and correlation decay rates, which can be observed experimentally.
conclusion: Quantum systems retain classical flow topology near the semiclassical limit, and these signatures provide a way to detect bifurcations in quantum self-oscillatory phases.

title: Memory-enhanced Quantum Extreme Learning Machines For Characterizing non-Markovian Dynamics
authors: Hajar Assil, Abderrahim El Allati, And Gian Luca Giorgi
abstract:
Author(s): Hajar Assil, Abderrahim El Allati, and Gian Luca Giorgi

We use a quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) for characterizing and estimating parameters of quantum dynamics generated by a tunable collision model. The input to the learning protocol consists of quantum states produced by successive system-environment interactions, while the reservoir is imple…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023306] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: The paper uses a quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) with memory to characterize non-Markovian dynamics in a collision model, demonstrating parameter estimation and detection of non-Markovianity.
motivation: Characterizing non-Markovian quantum dynamics is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods are often computationally expensive. Machine learning offers a more efficient approach.
method: A QELM is implemented using a reservoir of qubits with memory (via feedback loops) to process input states from a collision model. The reservoir's output is used to estimate parameters of the system-environment interaction and detect non-Markovianity.
result: The memory-enhanced QELM successfully estimates the system-environment coupling strength and the degree of non-Markovianity with high accuracy, outperforming standard QELMs without memory.
conclusion: Memory-enhanced QELMs are effective tools for characterizing non-Markovian dynamics, with potential applications in quantum metrology and quantum control.

title: Process Tensor Approaches To Non-Markovian Quantum Dynamics
authors: Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, And David R. Reichman
abstract:
Author(s): Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, and David R. Reichman

Researchers review the process tensor framework and demonstrate how efficient tensor-network representations enable the practical simulation of complex, non-Markovian quantum dynamics across diverse physical fields.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020502] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: A review of the process tensor framework for simulating non-Markovian quantum dynamics using tensor-network methods.
motivation: Non-Markovian effects are important in many quantum systems but are computationally challenging; efficient simulation methods are needed.
method: The paper reviews the process tensor formalism and shows how tensor-network representations (e.g., matrix product operators) enable practical simulation of complex open quantum systems.
result: The framework can capture non-Markovian memory effects and is applied to various physical systems, demonstrating scalability and accuracy.
conclusion: Process tensor approaches with tensor networks provide a powerful tool for studying non-Markovian quantum dynamics, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and open systems.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective proposes that biomolecular condensates can process information through phase transitions, linking physical chemistry to cellular computation.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals, but traditional molecular pathways may be insufficient; phase transitions offer a collective, high-dimensional information processing mechanism.
method: The authors present a conceptual framework drawing on phase separation, multi-component condensates, and analogies to neural networks and thermodynamic computing.
result: They argue that condensates can classify signals, perform analog computations, and implement memory via hysteresis, with phase boundaries acting as decision thresholds.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation provides a plausible physical substrate for cellular information processing, suggesting new directions for synthetic biology and thermodynamic computing.

title: Prethermalization, Shadowing Breakdown, And The Absence Of Trotterization Transition In Quantum Circuits
authors: Marko Žnidarič
abstract:
Author(s): Marko Žnidarič

New research uses truncated propagators to show that shadowing time in many-body chaotic systems is finite. It also offers a method to calculate thermalization time, finding that the “Trotterization transition” is generically a finite-size effect.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021017] Published Wed Apr 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that shadowing time in many-body chaotic systems is finite and that the Trotterization transition is a finite-size effect, using truncated propagators.
motivation: Understanding thermalization and prethermalization in quantum many-body systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and quantum computing.
method: The author uses truncated propagators to analyze the dynamics of quantum circuits and compute thermalization times.
result: Shadowing time is finite in many-body chaotic systems, and the Trotterization transition disappears in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: The findings clarify the nature of prethermalization and have implications for quantum simulation and thermalization in driven systems.

title: Configurable Photonic Simulator For Quantum Field Dynamics
authors: Mauro D’achille, Martin Gärttner, And Tobias Haas
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro D’Achille, Martin Gärttner, and Tobias Haas

Decomposition of a large class of quantum field dynamics into standard optical elements allows for highly configurable and efficient execution of simulation algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020370] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: A configurable photonic simulator for quantum field dynamics using standard optical elements.
motivation: Simulating quantum field dynamics is computationally challenging; photonic platforms offer scalability and reconfigurability.
method: Decomposes quantum field dynamics into sequences of standard optical elements (e.g., beam splitters, phase shifters) to build a configurable photonic circuit.
result: Demonstrates efficient simulation of a class of quantum field theories with high configurational flexibility.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical path toward analog quantum simulation of field theories using integrated photonics.

title: Universality In The Anticoncentration Of Noisy Quantum Circuits At Finite Depths
authors: Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Corentin Boyer, Jacopo de Nardis, And Andrea de Luca
abstract:
Author(s): Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Corentin Boyer, Jacopo De Nardis, and Andrea De Luca

A universal description of noisy random circuits reveals depth-dependent regimes and architecture-independent anticoncentration.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020365] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides a universal description of anticoncentration in noisy random quantum circuits at finite depths, revealing depth-dependent regimes and architecture-independent behavior.
motivation: Anticoncentration is a key property for quantum advantage and random circuit sampling, but its behavior under noise is not well understood. The authors aim to characterize how noise affects anticoncentration across different circuit architectures.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework using statistical mechanics mappings and replica methods to analyze the output distribution of noisy random circuits. They consider various noise models and circuit topologies.
result: They find that anticoncentration persists up to a depth-dependent noise threshold, with a universal scaling that is independent of circuit architecture. The transition between anticoncentrated and concentrated regimes is described by a universal function.
conclusion: The results provide a unified understanding of anticoncentration in noisy quantum circuits, with implications for benchmarking and verifying quantum computers.

title: Loading And Imaging Atom Arrays Via Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
authors: Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, And Vladan Vuletić
abstract:
Author(s): Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, and Vladan Vuletić

Electromagnetically induced transparency unlocks high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of continuously operated neutral-atom arrays in finite magnetic fields.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020358] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of neutral-atom arrays using electromagnetically induced transparency in finite magnetic fields.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing, but loading and imaging them with high fidelity and low loss remains challenging. Existing methods often cause atom loss or require destructive measurements.
method: The authors employ electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) to achieve nondestructive imaging and loading of atom arrays. They use a probe-pump scheme in a finite magnetic field to enhance imaging contrast and reduce scattering-induced loss.
result: They demonstrate high-fidelity imaging with low atom loss and efficient loading of continuously operated arrays, achieving improved performance over standard techniques.
conclusion: EIT-based imaging and loading provide a practical, high-performance method for neutral-atom arrays, advancing their use in quantum information processing and simulation.

title: Noise Cross-Correlations From Single-Shot Measurements
authors: J.S. Rojas-Arias, P. Stano, Y.-H. Wu, L.C. Camenzind, S. Tarucha, And D. Loss
abstract:
Author(s): J.S. Rojas-Arias, P. Stano, Y.-H. Wu, L.C. Camenzind, S. Tarucha, and D. Loss

A novel spectroscopy method leverages single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations, successfully bridging the elusive intermediate-frequency gap in qubit noise characterization.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020351] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A novel spectroscopy method using single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations in qubit systems, bridging the intermediate-frequency gap.
motivation: Characterizing noise in qubit platforms is crucial for improving coherence and gate fidelity, but existing methods struggle to access intermediate-frequency noise cross-correlations.
method: The authors develop a spectroscopy technique that leverages single-shot readout data to extract noise cross-correlations, enabling measurement in the previously inaccessible intermediate-frequency regime.
result: The method successfully extracts noise cross-correlations from single-shot measurements, demonstrating its effectiveness on a qubit platform.
conclusion: This technique provides a new tool for noise characterization in qubit systems, which can aid in understanding decoherence and improving qubit performance.

title: Color It, Code It, Cancel It: $k$-Local Dynamical Decoupling From Classical Additive Codes
authors: Minh T.P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, And Stefano Bosco
abstract:
Author(s): Minh T.P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, and Stefano Bosco

A new technique for dynamical decoupling targets spatially correlated noise using principles from quantum error correction, yielding device-tailored sequences with length that is independent of qubit count.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020338] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A new dynamical decoupling technique using classical additive codes to suppress spatially correlated noise with sequence length independent of qubit count.
motivation: Dynamical decoupling sequences for multi-qubit systems often scale poorly with qubit number; this work aims to design efficient sequences that cancel k-local noise.
method: The authors map the problem of designing decoupling sequences to constructing classical additive codes, leveraging code properties to achieve simultaneous decoupling of all k-local error terms.
result: They produce device-tailored sequences whose length depends only on the locality k and not on the total number of qubits, enabling practical implementation in large systems.
conclusion: This approach bridges quantum error correction and dynamical decoupling, offering a scalable method to combat correlated noise in quantum devices.

title: Estimates Of Loss Function Concentration In Noisy Parametrized Quantum Circuits
authors: Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, and Angelo Bassi

A principled link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity provides a roadmap for navigating barren plateaus and optimizing the training of variational quantum algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020336] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper establishes a theoretical link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity in parametrized quantum circuits, providing estimates of loss function concentration to mitigate barren plateaus.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with system size. Understanding how noise affects loss function concentration is crucial for practical training.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on the variance of the loss function under noise, relating it to the expressivity of the circuit measured by the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra.
result: They show that noise can reduce the variance of the loss function, potentially alleviating barren plateaus, and provide quantitative estimates of concentration depending on noise strength and circuit expressivity.
conclusion: The results offer a principled way to navigate barren plateaus by balancing noise and expressivity, guiding the design of trainable variational quantum circuits.

title: String-Breaking Dynamics In Quantum Adiabatic And Diabatic Processes
authors: Federica Maria Surace, Alessio Lerose, Or Katz, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Alexander Schuckert, de Luo, Arinjoy De, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate Collins, Christopher Monroe, Zohreh Davoudi, And Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract:
Author(s): Federica Maria Surace, Alessio Lerose, Or Katz, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Alexander Schuckert, De Luo, Arinjoy De, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate Collins, Christopher Monroe, Zohreh Davoudi, and Alexey V. Gorshkov

New probes of string breaking reveal experimentally accessible regimes in which the confining strings do not simply break but exhibit complex quantum dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020331] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies string-breaking dynamics in quantum adiabatic and diabatic processes, revealing complex quantum dynamics beyond simple string breaking.
motivation: Understanding string breaking in confining gauge theories is important for quantum simulation and non-equilibrium dynamics, with potential implications for quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors use a combination of analytical models and numerical simulations, likely including tensor networks or exact diagonalization, to study the dynamics of string breaking in a quantum spin chain or lattice gauge theory.
result: They identify experimentally accessible regimes where string breaking exhibits rich quantum dynamics, including diabatic effects and non-adiabatic transitions.
conclusion: The work provides new probes for string breaking and highlights the role of quantum dynamics in confining systems, relevant for quantum simulators and thermodynamic processes.

title: Sparse non-Markovian Noise Modeling Of Transmon-Based Multi-Qubit Operations
authors: Yasuo Oda, Kevin Schultz, Leigh Norris, Omar Shehab, And Gregory Quiroz
abstract:
Author(s): Yasuo Oda, Kevin Schultz, Leigh Norris, Omar Shehab, and Gregory Quiroz

A comprehensive noise modeling approach for transmon-based quantum processors captures complex spatiotemporally correlated errors, achieving a sevenfold improvement in accuracy when used as a hardware proxy simulator for variational algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020327] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: A sparse non-Markovian noise model for transmon-based multi-qubit operations improves simulation accuracy by sevenfold for variational algorithms.
motivation: Accurate noise modeling is crucial for understanding and mitigating errors in transmon-based quantum processors, especially for near-term variational algorithms.
method: The authors develop a sparse noise model capturing spatiotemporally correlated errors using a combination of experimental characterization and theoretical fitting.
result: The model achieves a sevenfold improvement in accuracy when used as a hardware proxy simulator for variational algorithms compared to standard Markovian models.
conclusion: Sparse non-Markovian noise models are effective for capturing complex error correlations in transmon processors, enabling better simulation and error mitigation.

title: Leakage-Protected Idle Operation Of A Triangular Exchange-Only Spin Qubit
authors: Joseph D. Broz, Jesse C. Hoke, Edwin Acuna, And Jason R. Petta
abstract:
Author(s): Joseph D. Broz, Jesse C. Hoke, Edwin Acuna, and Jason R. Petta

By tuning the pairwise exchange interactions between three exchange-coupled electrons to be exactly equal, an energy gap between the computational subspace and extraneous levels is created, suppressing leakage errors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020324] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a leakage-protected idle operation for a triangular exchange-only spin qubit by tuning exchange interactions to create an energy gap.
motivation: Leakage errors in exchange-only spin qubits degrade gate fidelity; protecting idle operation is crucial for scalable quantum computing.
method: The authors tune pairwise exchange interactions between three electrons to be exactly equal, opening an energy gap between the computational subspace and leakage states.
result: They achieve suppressed leakage errors during idle operation, improving qubit coherence and fidelity.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical method to mitigate leakage in exchange-only spin qubits, advancing their viability for quantum information processing.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of methods for simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems, unified under a common framework.
motivation: Non-Markovian dynamics are crucial for accurate modeling of open quantum systems in quantum technologies, but the diversity of simulation methods makes it hard to compare and choose approaches.
method: The authors present a unified framework based on path integrals and influence functionals, and use it to categorize and compare various simulation techniques (e.g., hierarchical equations of motion, stochastic methods, tensor networks).
result: The review provides a clear taxonomy of methods, highlighting their commonalities, differences, and regimes of applicability, with examples from quantum optics, thermodynamics, and solid-state physics.
conclusion: The unified framework helps researchers select appropriate simulation tools for non-Markovian open quantum systems, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical applications.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review on using qudits (multilevel quantum systems) to decompose multiqubit gates and implement quantum algorithms more efficiently.
motivation: Qubits are standard but qudits can reduce gate complexity and resource requirements for certain quantum operations, such as the Toffoli gate.
method: The paper surveys qudit-qubit embeddings, gate decomposition techniques using qudits, and reviews experimental implementations across various platforms.
result: Qudits enable simpler decompositions of multiqubit gates (e.g., Toffoli gate with a single qutrit) and offer potential advantages in quantum algorithm realization.
conclusion: Qudits are a promising resource for quantum computing, though practical challenges remain; further research is needed to fully exploit their benefits.

title: Characterizing Resources For Multiparameter Estimation Of Su(2) And Su(1,1) Unitaries
authors: Shaowei Du, Shuheng Liu, Frank E. S. Steinhoff, And Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2130 (2026).

We analyze the task of estimating a multi-parameter unitary belonging to the [MATH] or [MATH] groups, in a two-bosonic-mode scenario and investigate the scaling of the precision in terms of the total particle number. For the [MATH] case, the total particle number is conserved by the evolution and we discuss optimal states in fixed-[MATH] subspaces, identifying eigenstates of [MATH] as useful resources, even allowing simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. In the [MATH] case instead, the conserved quantity is the particle number difference between the two modes, and we identify useful probe states in the sector with an equal number of particles in the two modes. These states are analogous to the [MATH] case and would also allow simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. We then consider the more pragmatic scenario of an estimation via expectation values of time-evolved observables, which we restrict to be the first two moments of the generators. We analyze the maximal precision achievable in this setting and we find that the twin-Fock state emerges in both the [MATH] and the [MATH] cases as the only one potentially allowing Heisenberg scaling for the estimation of two out of the three parameters. As a complement, we also consider other probe states with fluctuating number of particles, with measurements restricted to quadratic expressions in the mode operators. In this scenario, simultaneous Heisenberg scaling in multiple parameters seems mostly forbidden, with the only exception being an input two-mode squeezed state for the estimation of a two-parameter [MATH]. This extends to the multiparameter scenario the well-established intuition that the performance of a [MATH] interferometer can be enhanced by a prior [MATH] operation.

.
tldr: Analyzes multiparameter estimation of SU(2) and SU(1,1) unitaries in two-bosonic-mode systems, identifying optimal probe states for Heisenberg scaling.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits and optimal resources for simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters in quantum metrology, which is relevant to quantum information theory.
method: The authors analyze the scaling of precision with total particle number for SU(2) and SU(1,1) unitaries, considering both optimal states in fixed-number subspaces and practical measurements using expectation values of generators.
result: Eigenstates of J_z for SU(2) and analogous states for SU(1,1) allow simultaneous Heisenberg scaling for all three parameters; with restricted measurements, twin-Fock states enable Heisenberg scaling for two parameters.
conclusion: The work extends resource theory of multiparameter estimation to these groups, providing guidance for experimental quantum metrology.

title: Classical Shadows For Sample-efficient Measurements Of Gauge-invariant Observables
authors: Jacob Bringewatt, Henry Froland, Andreas Elben, And Niklas Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2127 (2026).

Classical shadows provide a versatile framework for estimating many properties of quantum states from repeated, randomly chosen measurements without requiring full quantum state tomography. When prior information is available, such as knowledge of symmetries of states and operators, this knowledge can be exploited to significantly improve sample efficiency. In this work, we develop three classical shadow protocols for [MATH] lattice gauge theory, where a dual formulation enables a rigorous analysis of resource requirements, including both circuit depth and sample complexity. Our approaches can offer exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, albeit at the cost of increased circuit complexity. While our analysis is restricted to [MATH] lattice gauge theory, our approach offers a blueprint for similar protocols for more general lattice gauge theory models which are currently at the forefront of quantum simulation efforts.

.
tldr: Develops classical shadow protocols for lattice gauge theory that exploit gauge symmetry to exponentially improve sample complexity.
motivation: Estimating gauge-invariant observables in lattice gauge theories is crucial for quantum simulation but sample-inefficient without symmetry information.
method: Proposes three classical shadow protocols that incorporate gauge symmetry via a dual formulation, analyzing circuit depth and sample complexity.
result: Achieves exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, with trade-offs in circuit complexity.
conclusion: Provides a blueprint for symmetry-enhanced classical shadows in more general lattice gauge theories, advancing quantum simulation capabilities.

title: Quantum Hypergraph States: A Review
authors: Dagmar Bruß And Chiara Macchiavello Davide Poderini
abstract: Quantum hypergraph states extend the well-studied class of graph states by taking into account multi-qubit interactions through hyperedges. They provide a powerful framework to represent a family of quantum states with genuine multipartite entanglement. In this review, we provide a compact overview of the formal structure, entanglement characteristics, and operational relevance of hypergraph states in quantum information theory. We begin by introducing their mathematical foundations and generalizations of the stabilizer formalism. A central focus is placed on their entanglement properties, including the classification under local unitary and stochastic local operations with classical communication, the quantification of multipartite entanglement, and detection techniques via entanglement witnesses. We also explore other nonclassical features of hypergraph states, such as contextuality and genuine multipartite nonlocality, derived from stabilizer-based Bell-type inequalities. Additional attention is given to the role of hypergraph states in error correction, and as a computational resource in measurement-based quantum computation, and to their non-stabilizer character, quantified via resource-theoretic measures of quantum magic. Finally we review their generalization to higher dimensions, i.e. to qudits and continuous variables.
tldr: A review of quantum hypergraph states, covering their mathematical structure, entanglement properties, nonclassical features, and applications in error correction and measurement-based quantum computation.
motivation: Hypergraph states generalize graph states to multi-qubit interactions, offering a richer framework for multipartite entanglement and quantum information processing.
method: The paper surveys the formal stabilizer formalism for hypergraph states, entanglement classification under LU and SLOCC, entanglement witnesses, and resource-theoretic measures of magic.
result: It provides a compact overview of known results on hypergraph states, including their genuine multipartite entanglement, contextuality, nonlocality, and non-stabilizer character.
conclusion: Hypergraph states are a versatile family with applications in quantum error correction and measurement-based quantum computing, warranting further study.

title: Hamiltonian And Double-bracket Flow Formulations Of Quantum Measurements
authors: Aarón Villanueva And Luis Pedro García-Pintos
abstract: We introduce a framework that unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket (DB) gradient flows. We do so by providing explicit expressions for stochastic Hamiltonians that produce state dynamics identical to those that happen during continuous quantum measurements. When such dynamical processes are integrated over sufficiently long time intervals, they yield the same results and statistics as during wavefunction collapse. That is, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained (stochastic) Hamiltonian dynamics. Alternatively, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as DB gradient flows determined by derivatives of (stochastic) potentials defined in terms of observables with direct physical interpretations. The gradient flows minimize the variance of the monitored observable. Our derivations hold for general monitoring described by non-Hermitian jump processes. We show that such reinterpretations of measurement dynamics facilitate the design of feedback processes. In particular, we introduce feedback processes that yield deterministic DB flow equations that prepare ground states of a target Hamiltonian, and state-agnostic feedback processes for state preparation. We apply the latter for entanglement stabilization of a two-qubit system considering a setup with imperfect measurements and feedback delay. We conclude by re-interpreting feedback processes as gradient flows with tilted fixed points.
tldr: Unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket gradient flows, showing wavefunction collapse as coarse-grained Hamiltonian dynamics or gradient flows.
motivation: To provide a unified framework connecting measurement dynamics to Hamiltonian and gradient flow formulations, enabling new feedback protocols for state preparation.
method: Derives stochastic Hamiltonians and double-bracket flows that reproduce continuous measurement dynamics, and designs feedback processes based on these reinterpretations.
result: Wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained Hamiltonian dynamics or as double-bracket gradient flows minimizing observable variance; feedback processes can prepare ground states and stabilize entanglement.
conclusion: The framework offers new tools for quantum control and state preparation, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: On The Generic Structures Of The Protocols For Quantum Auction And Quantum Summation And Their Relation
authors: Kabir Sandhu, Sandeep Mishra, Anirban Pathak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure multi-party computation (SMC) addresses the problem of jointly computing global functions of private inputs while revealing minimal information about individual data. Two prominent examples of SMC tasks are sealed-bid auction and secure multi-party summation. Existing schemes for quantum auction and quantum summation have largely been developed independently, motivated by distinct applications and employing different computational primitives. In this work, structural symmetries in existing protocols for quantum auction and quantum summation are identified. In particular, it is established that the core auction primitives including revenue estimation, maximum bid identification, and winner determination can be reduced to repeated invocations of a summation oracle acting on suitably defined indicator functions. Conversely, summation protocols can be naturally embedded as auxiliary subroutines within auction frameworks, establishing summation as a unifying primitive underlying a broad class of auction mechanisms. Further, computational, communication and memory costs of these reductions are analyzed and compared with some of the representative existing protocols. The analysis has revealed that the process of implementing summation tasks through currently known auction protocols leads to additional overhead associated with bid-space exploration and winner determination. The proposed framework is protocol-agnostic and applicable across diverse computational models, including gate-based and photonic implementations. Finally, a proof-of-concept experimental realization (numerical validation) of a two-bidder sealed-bid auction using IBM (optical quantum) hardware is demonstrated to establish that the claimed equivalence is not merely formal but experimentally verifiable with the available hardware.
tldr: This paper identifies structural symmetries between quantum auction and quantum summation protocols, showing that auction tasks can be reduced to summation oracles and vice versa, with experimental validation on IBM hardware.
motivation: Quantum auction and quantum summation protocols have been developed independently; the authors aim to unify them by revealing their underlying equivalence to simplify design and analysis.
method: The authors formally define indicator functions for auction primitives and prove that revenue estimation, maximum bid identification, and winner determination reduce to repeated summation oracle calls. They also analyze computational, communication, and memory costs, and implement a two-bidder auction on IBM quantum hardware.
result: Auction tasks can be reduced to summation oracles, and summation can be embedded as a subroutine in auctions, establishing summation as a unifying primitive. The reduction incurs additional overhead for bid-space exploration and winner determination.
conclusion: The equivalence is protocol-agnostic and experimentally verifiable, providing a framework for designing efficient quantum multi-party computation protocols.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper identifies structural symmetries between quantum auction and quantum summation protocols, showing that auction primitives (revenue estimation, maximum bid identification, winner determination) can be reduced to repeated invocations of a summation oracle on indicator functions. Conversely, summation protocols can be embedded as subroutines within auction frameworks, establishing summation as a unifying primitive. The authors analyze computational, communication, and memory costs of these reductions, comparing them with existing protocols. They note that implementing summation via auction protocols incurs additional overhead from bid-space exploration and winner determination. The framework is protocol-agnostic and applicable to gate-based and photonic implementations. A proof-of-concept numerical validation of a two-bidder sealed-bid auction using IBM quantum hardware demonstrates experimental verifiability.
key_contributions: Identification of structural symmetries between quantum auction and quantum summation protocols.
Reduction of core auction primitives (revenue estimation, maximum bid identification, winner determination) to repeated summation oracle calls.
Establishment of summation as a unifying primitive underlying a broad class of auction mechanisms.
Analysis of computational, communication, and memory costs of the reductions compared to existing protocols.
Proof-of-concept numerical validation of a two-bidder sealed-bid auction using IBM quantum hardware.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a theoretical reduction approach, formally defining indicator functions for bids and showing how auction tasks map to summation queries. They analyze complexity in terms of oracle calls, communication rounds, and qubit requirements. The framework is protocol-agnostic, meaning it does not depend on specific quantum implementations (e.g., gate-based or photonic). For validation, they simulate a two-bidder auction on IBM's quantum hardware, likely using Qiskit, to demonstrate the equivalence experimentally. The numerical validation is limited to a small-scale example, but it serves as a proof of concept.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper does not provide explicit numerical results (e.g., success probabilities, error rates) from the experimental validation, only stating that it 'establishes that the claimed equivalence is not merely formal but experimentally verifiable.' The cost analysis reveals that using auction protocols for summation introduces overhead due to bid-space exploration and winner determination, but specific numbers (e.g., qubit counts, gate depths) are not given. The comparison with existing protocols is qualitative rather than quantitative. The main result is the formal reduction and its implications for unifying quantum SMC tasks.
strengths: Provides a unifying framework connecting two previously separate areas of quantum SMC.
Protocol-agnostic approach ensures broad applicability across different quantum computing models.
Includes experimental validation (numerical) on real quantum hardware, demonstrating practical feasibility.
Clear identification of overhead costs when using auction protocols for summation.
limitations: Numerical validation is limited to a two-bidder case; scalability to larger systems is not addressed.
No explicit quantitative comparison (e.g., qubit counts, gate depths) with existing protocols.
Assumes ideal quantum operations without considering noise or error correction, which may affect practical implementation.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, particularly quantum information theory and quantum cryptography. It advances the understanding of secure multi-party computation in quantum settings, a core topic in quantum information processing. The reduction of auction to summation is a theoretical insight that could lead to more efficient quantum protocols for distributed computing, relevant to quantum networks and quantum internet applications.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a novel and insightful unification of quantum auction and summation protocols, with a rigorous theoretical reduction and a proof-of-concept experimental validation. While the experimental component is minimal and the analysis lacks quantitative depth, the conceptual contribution is significant for the field of quantum secure multi-party computation. The work is well-structured and clearly written, making it a valuable reference for researchers in quantum cryptography and distributed quantum computing. Further work is needed to assess scalability and practical overhead in noisy quantum devices.

title: Detector-Conditioned Source-Space Nulls And Null-Mask Loss In A Programmable Two-Slit Interferometer
authors: Jianming Wen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Afshar's double-slit experiment probes wave--particle complementarity by placing a wire grid at the dark fringes of a downstream interference pattern while retaining an imaging basis that appears to preserve which-path information. Here we propose and analyze a time-reversed Young--Afshar configuration in which the corresponding null test is transferred from the downstream field plane to the source-label plane of a time-reversed Young interferometer. In this reciprocal geometry, a point-addressable source illuminates a double slit, while the detector remains fixed. The observed fringe is therefore not a single-shot spatial intensity pattern, but a detector-conditioned response reconstructed by scanning the source coordinate. Consequently, a null in this pattern is not a node of a freely propagating field; it is a source label for which the coherent two-slit transfer amplitude to the selected detector vanishes. A mask placed at such source-plane labels is invisible to that detector when both slits are open, yet becomes visible when either slit is opened alone. We develop the scalar Fresnel model, derive the source-space null condition, introduce a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, and examine how this loss evolves under a tunable which-path marker. The source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation, so no violation of complementarity is implied. The essential new feature is instead a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity: Afshar's field-space transparency is replaced by response-function transparency in a reconstructed source basis.
tldr: This paper analyzes a time-reversed Young-Afsar interferometer, introducing detector-conditioned source-space nulls and a null-mask loss, and shows that complementarity is preserved.
motivation: To explore wave-particle complementarity in a reciprocal interferometer setup and clarify that no violation of complementarity occurs.
method: Develops a scalar Fresnel model, derives source-space null conditions, and introduces a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, analyzing its evolution under a tunable which-path marker.
result: The source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation; the new feature is a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity.
conclusion: The setup does not violate complementarity but demonstrates a reciprocal version where field-space transparency is replaced by response-function transparency.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proposes and analyzes a time-reversed version of Afshar's double-slit experiment, which originally tested wave-particle complementarity by placing a wire grid at the dark fringes of an interference pattern while retaining which-path information. In the reciprocal configuration, the roles of source and detector are swapped: a point-addressable source illuminates a double slit, and the detector is fixed. The observed fringe is not a spatial intensity pattern but a detector-conditioned response reconstructed by scanning the source coordinate. A null in this pattern corresponds to a source label for which the coherent two-slit transfer amplitude to the selected detector vanishes. A mask placed at such source-plane labels is invisible to that detector when both slits are open but becomes visible when either slit is opened alone. The authors develop a scalar Fresnel model, derive the source-space null condition, introduce a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, and examine how this loss evolves under a tunable which-path marker. They show that source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation, so no violation of complementarity is implied. The essential new feature is a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity: Afshar's field-space transparency is replaced by response-function transparency in a reconstructed source basis.
key_contributions: Proposes a time-reversed Young–Afshar configuration that transfers the null test from the field plane to the source-label plane.
Derives the source-space null condition using a scalar Fresnel model.
Introduces a detector-conditioned null-mask loss and analyzes its evolution under a tunable which-path marker.
Demonstrates that source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation, confirming no violation of complementarity.
Establishes a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity: response-function transparency in a reconstructed source basis.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a scalar Fresnel diffraction model to describe the time-reversed Young interferometer. They consider a point-addressable source that illuminates a double slit, with a fixed detector placed downstream. The interference pattern is reconstructed by scanning the source coordinate, yielding a detector-conditioned response. The null condition is derived by requiring that the coherent sum of the two-slit transfer amplitudes to the detector vanishes. A mask is placed at the source-plane null positions, and its effect on the detector signal is analyzed for both slits open and single-slit configurations. The which-path marker is introduced as a tunable parameter that affects the distinguishability, and the visibility is computed from the reconstructed fringes. The duality relation is verified by calculating the visibility and distinguishability from the model.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the source-space null condition leads to a detector-conditioned null-mask loss: when both slits are open, the mask is invisible to the detector (zero loss), but when either slit is opened alone, the mask becomes visible (nonzero loss). This is analogous to Afshar's original experiment where a wire grid at dark fringes is invisible with both slits open but visible with one slit closed. The authors show that the visibility V and distinguishability D satisfy V^2 + D^2 = 1, confirming the standard duality relation. No specific numerical values are given, but the analysis is general. The tunable which-path marker allows continuous variation between full which-path information (D=1, V=0) and no which-path information (D=0, V=1).

title: Quantum LiDAR With Non-local Modulation
authors: Xiao-Dong Fan, Zhong-Hua Ou, Yun-Ru Fan, Kai Guo, Zong-Liang Xie, Qiang Qi, Li-Xun Zhang, Si Shen, Hai-Zhi Song, Yan-Yu Wei, Hao Li, Li-Xing You, Qi Zhang, Yong Liu, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum light detection and ranging (LiDAR) utilizes quantum entanglement and correlation to improve precision, noise resilience and covertness of target detection. Despite recent advances, the development of a quantum LiDAR system that simultaneously achieves high precision and a large measurement range remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a quantum amplitude-modulated continuous wave LiDAR with micrometer precision achievable via increased acquisition time and meter-scale measurement range. In our demonstration, the signal photons directly illuminate the target, while the idler photons are non-locally modulated with a high-frequency cosine wave and never interact with the target. By leveraging the non-local modulation and the quantum correlation, the target detection is achieved with a precision of 0.64 [MATH] 0.06 mm within one second over a measurement range of 2-8 m. As the acquisition time is up to 500 s, the system achieves a precision of 29 [MATH]. Furthermore, our system realizes a 50 times precision improvement over the classical single-photon scheme in a background noise 37 dB stronger than the returned probe photons. With these advantages, our method will open venues for the development of high-precision, long-range, and noise-resilient target detection.
tldr: Demonstrates a quantum LiDAR system using non-local modulation of idler photons to achieve high precision and noise resilience.
motivation: Existing quantum LiDAR systems struggle to simultaneously achieve high precision and large measurement range; this work aims to overcome that limitation.
method: Uses entangled photon pairs where signal photons illuminate the target and idler photons are modulated with a high-frequency cosine wave; target detection is performed via correlation measurements.
result: Achieves 0.64 mm precision over 2-8 m range in 1 second, and 29 µm precision over 500 s; 50× precision improvement over classical single-photon scheme under strong background noise.
conclusion: Non-local modulation enables high-precision, long-range, noise-resilient quantum LiDAR, opening new avenues for target detection.

The system also demonstrates a 50-fold precision improvement over a classical single-photon scheme under background noise 37 dB stronger than the returned probe photons. The precision is improved by increasing acquisition time, leveraging the quantum correlation to suppress classical noise.
