method: The authors define s-plateaued partitions, analyze possible cardinalities, provide explicit constructions ensuring no nonzero linear structure, and characterize such partitions for odd m with specific parameters.
result: They show that for certain parameters, the preimage set partition of a plateaued function is an s-plateaued partition iff the function is of a specific form, and partially address an open problem on bent partitions.
conclusion: The work generalizes bent partitions and provides tools for constructing plateaued functions, but the results are primarily combinatorial and algebraic, with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Structure-Preserving Neural-Spectral Method For Reconstructing Controls Of Wave Equations
authors: Tan-Phuc Nguyen, Minh-Binh Tran, Son Tu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The numerical reconstruction of controls for partial differential equations remains comparatively underdeveloped, despite the extensive analytical literature on controllability. This difficulty is particularly pronounced for wave equations, whose conservative structure, oscillatory dynamics, and high-frequency behavior make direct discretization and optimization challenging. In this work, we introduce a Neural-Spectral method for approximating controls of wave equations. The method represents both the state and the control in a Dirichlet spectral basis and parameterizes the time-dependent modal coefficients using shallow neural networks. In this way, the spatial oscillatory structure of the wave equation is built into the approximation, and the learning task is reduced to reconstructing temporal coefficients. We prove approximation results showing that, under the standing assumption that an exact control exists in the relevant energy framework, the control-state pairs found can approximate exact controlled trajectories uniformly in time in the energy norm, while also approximating the corresponding controls in \(L^2\). We also state a conditional computable error estimate that separates spectral truncation, neural-network approximation, quadrature, and optimization errors. In addition, we discuss structural obstructions faced by standard time-stepping schemes for conservative wave dynamics: explicit Euler amplifies high frequencies, implicit Euler introduces artificial dissipation, and Crank--Nicolson preserves amplitudes but compresses high-frequency phases. Numerical experiments in one, two, and three space dimensions illustrate the method on nonlinear, linear-reference, and high-dimensional control benchmarks.
tldr: A neural-spectral method for reconstructing controls of wave equations, combining spectral decomposition with shallow neural networks.
motivation: Numerical reconstruction of controls for wave equations is underdeveloped due to their conservative, oscillatory nature; standard time-stepping schemes face structural obstructions.
method: Represent state and control in a Dirichlet spectral basis and parameterize time-dependent modal coefficients using shallow neural networks, reducing the learning task to temporal coefficient reconstruction.
result: Proves approximation results showing control-state pairs approximate exact controlled trajectories uniformly in energy norm and controls in L^2; provides conditional computable error estimates.
conclusion: The method effectively handles nonlinear, linear-reference, and high-dimensional control benchmarks in 1D, 2D, and 3D, overcoming limitations of standard time-stepping schemes.

title: Performance Analysis And Optimal Design Of ORB-Type Grand Algorithms
authors: Wenyi Zhang Li Wan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Guessing Random Additive Noise Decoding (GRAND) performs decoding by sequentially guessing channel error patterns (EPs). Ordered Reliability Bits GRAND (ORBGRAND) is a notable instance suitable for efficient implementation, as it schedules EPs solely according to the ranking of soft channel outputs. In this paper, we generalize this principle to a broader class of GRAND algorithms whose testing order depends only on reliability ranking, referred to as ORB-type GRAND. We develop a unified analytical framework based on a key quantity termed the average guessing posterior (AGP), which captures the effectiveness of each EP and reduces decoding into an ordering problem over the EP space. For random code ensembles, we derive exact expressions for the block error rate (BLER), stopping-time distribution, and average number of tests under a fixed test budget. The analysis separates target-miss and target-preemption errors and shows that ordering EPs by non-increasing AGP is optimal over the EP set under consideration. For fixed linear block codes, we derive the BLER expression that isolates the code-dependent target-preemption term and characterize this term through higher-order weight relationships of codeword tuples, with a computable first-order upper bound as a useful special case. Guided by these insights, we formulate ReShuffled-ORBGRAND (RS-ORBGRAND) as an offline AGP-based reshuffling scheme. Numerical results for the Bose--Chaudhuri--Hocquenghem (BCH)[MATH] code show that RS-ORBGRAND consistently improves existing ORB-type GRAND algorithms and lies within [MATH]~dB of a maximum-likelihood decoding lower-bound benchmark at a BLER of [MATH].
tldr: This paper analyzes and optimizes ORB-type GRAND decoding algorithms for classical error correction, focusing on performance metrics and optimal design.
motivation: To improve the efficiency and performance of GRAND-based decoding algorithms for classical linear block codes.
method: Develops a unified analytical framework using average guessing posterior (AGP) to characterize decoding performance, and proposes RS-ORBGRAND as an offline reshuffling scheme.
result: Derives exact expressions for block error rate and stopping-time distribution, and shows RS-ORBGRAND improves existing ORB-type GRAND algorithms, approaching maximum-likelihood decoding.
conclusion: The AGP-based ordering is optimal for ORB-type GRAND, and RS-ORBGRAND offers a practical improvement with performance close to ML decoding.

title: A Fast sum-of-Gaussians Algorithm For The High-dimensional Fractional Fokker-Planck Equation
authors: Shidong Jiang, Dong Wang, Qi Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a fast, high-order algorithm for the free-space fractional Fokker-Planck equation (FFPE) in arbitrary spatial dimension. Its fundamental solution, corresponding to a Dirac-delta initial condition, is obtained from the explicit Fourier representation by applying a sum-of-Gaussians (SOG) approximation to the nonseparable stretched exponential, using its complete monotonicity as the Laplace transform of a one-sided [MATH]-stable density. Each Gaussian term is an ordinary heat kernel and therefore factorizes across spatial coordinates. On a tensor-product grid, the separated form can be assembled in [MATH] work and storage, rather than forming all [MATH] grid values, where [MATH] is the number of Gaussian terms and [MATH] is the number of points per dimension. We prove an a~priori error estimate for the pure-fractional fundamental solution and give a parameter-selection procedure for prescribed accuracy over specified ranges of space and time. In numerical experiments the method achieves more than ten digits of relative accuracy, with [MATH] growing only logarithmically in the inverse tolerance, and maintains this accuracy in dimensions up to [MATH]. This exceeds the dimensions reached in comparable radial-quadrature tests, where the integrand becomes increasingly oscillatory as the dimension grows. Because the method represents the fundamental solution as a separated sum of heat kernels, any initial datum given as a finite sum of tensor products can be evolved in closed form using only one-dimensional convolutions. This yields a computable class of high-dimensional solutions that is amenable to error analysis, and tensor neural networks provide one possible way to construct such separated representations for more general data.
tldr: A fast sum-of-Gaussians algorithm for solving the high-dimensional fractional Fokker-Planck equation.
motivation: Efficiently solve the fractional Fokker-Planck equation in high dimensions, which is computationally challenging due to non-separable stretched exponential kernels.
method: Approximates the fundamental solution via a sum-of-Gaussians (SOG) representation, exploiting complete monotonicity and Laplace transform; each Gaussian factorizes across dimensions, enabling tensor-product grid methods.
result: Achieves over ten digits of relative accuracy with logarithmic growth in the number of Gaussian terms, and scales to dimensions up to 100, outperforming radial-quadrature methods.
conclusion: The SOG method provides a practical, high-order algorithm for high-dimensional fractional diffusion, with potential extensions via tensor neural networks for general initial data.

title: The Multiply Iterated Law Of The Iterated Logarithm: Game-theoretic Foundations Of Sequential Detection Boundaries
authors: Akshay Balsubramani
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anytime-valid confidence sequences and e-processes are built almost universally from one recipe: average exponential test statistics over a prior on the tilting scale, then invoke Ville's inequality on the resulting nonnegative supermartingale. The mixing prior sets the width of the detection boundary and is usually chosen by hand. We recast the recipe as a two-player game with information as currency. A Learner commits to the prior; Nature adaptively produces a mean-zero score process whose difficulty is priced by a cumulant-generating-function charge. The Learner's mixture wealth obeys a single pathwise Gibbs-variational identity that holds along every realized path with no expectation operator; Ville's inequality, the equalizer condition, the GROW characterization, and the saddlepoint formula are all specializations of it. Three messages organize the rest. First, the law of the iterated logarithm (LIL) is the minimax boundary of this sequential-detection game, not arbitrary combinatorial slack. Second, the optimal prior is not a design choice but the forced equalizer strategy -- the unique law that makes every boundary-crossing time equally costly for Nature -- and it yields the sharp first iterated-log correction in closed form, with coefficient 3/2 = 1 + 1/2 (one for the Erds baseline, one half for the Laplace envelope around the saddle). Third, in the log-log scale chart the equalizer is exactly the Jeffreys prior on the scale-of-scales. The Erds-Kolmogorov integral test is the criterion that selects it. The two-stage finite-time LIL proof, the Howard-Ramdas mixture and stitching constructions, and betting confidence sequences all read as instances of this equalizer principle. A companion empirical evaluation confirms the central identities and locates the Erds threshold at the predicted value.
tldr: This paper develops a game-theoretic foundation for sequential detection boundaries, showing that the law of the iterated logarithm emerges as the minimax boundary and the optimal prior is the Jeffreys prior.
motivation: To provide a unified, game-theoretic framework for anytime-valid confidence sequences and e-processes, removing the need for ad-hoc prior selection.
method: The paper recasts the standard mixture recipe as a two-player game between Learner and Nature, using a pathwise Gibbs-variational identity to derive optimal strategies.
result: The law of the iterated logarithm is shown to be the minimax boundary of the sequential detection game, and the optimal equalizer prior yields the sharp first iterated-log correction with coefficient 3/2.
conclusion: The game-theoretic perspective unifies existing constructions (Howard-Ramdas mixture, stitching, betting) and provides a principled way to derive optimal detection boundaries.

title: Analysis Of Nonlinear Random Polarization In Dispersive Dielectrics
authors: Emmanuel E. Oguadimma Nathan L. Gibson
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a study on the time-domain propagation of electromagnetic waves in dielectric materials modeled by a nonlinear Debye medium with random perturbations. Polynomial Chaos Expansions are employed to transform the random nonlinear Debye polarization model into a deterministic framework. We extend the Yee discretization to the resulting coupled system, establish second order accuracy, and verify convergence numerically. We investigate the sensitivity of nonlinear properties to uncertainty, particularly when the amplitude of the input signal is large. Given the challenges in manufacturing where uncertainties can cause optimal parameters to vary and potentially disrupt nonlinear effects, our approach incorporates these uncertainties within the simulation. This can enable the model-based design identification of realizable materials that maintain their desired effects despite variations. The findings from this study contribute to a deeper understanding of wave propagation in complex media, with potential implications for applications in optical communications, material science, and electromagnetic wave control.
tldr: This paper studies nonlinear random polarization in dispersive dielectrics using polynomial chaos expansions and numerical simulations, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand wave propagation in complex dielectric media with random perturbations, which is relevant for optical communications and material science.
method: Polynomial Chaos Expansions are used to transform the random nonlinear Debye polarization model into a deterministic system, and the Yee discretization is extended to solve the coupled equations with second-order accuracy.
result: The method converges numerically and allows sensitivity analysis of nonlinear properties to uncertainty, particularly for large input signals.
conclusion: The approach enables model-based design of materials that maintain desired nonlinear effects despite manufacturing uncertainties.

title: Operator Learning For Cubic Nonlinear Schr\"odinger Equation On Periodic Domains
authors: Emmanuel E. Oguadimma, Victory C. Obieke, Xueying Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the cubic nonlinear Schr\"odinger (NLS) equation on two-dimensional flat tori with varying aspect ratios. In this formulation, the choice of aspect ratio governs the Fourier resonance structure, so rational and irrational geometries can exhibit different high-frequency cascade behaviors. We present a geometry-conditioned Fourier neural operator (FNO) for the cubic defocusing NLS equation, where the input consists of the real and imaginary parts of the solution together with the aspect-ratio parameter \(\omega^2\). The model is trained to approximate the one-step solution operator and is evaluated on unseen trajectories generated from random-phase initial data using Fourier pseudospectral method. Our numerical experiments show that the learned operator captures the main solution dynamics on both tori and reproduces the distinct Sobolev norm behavior of the two geometries, with stronger \(H^2\)-growth on the rational torus and more constrained behavior on the irrational torus, consistent with the findings of . We perform ablation studies to examine the roles of retained Fourier modes, activation functions, Fourier-layer depth, and explicit geometry conditioning. The results indicate that including [MATH] improves long-time predictive accuracy, especially for the rational geometry, and supports the use of geometry-aware neural operators for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive partial differential equations.
tldr: This paper uses a Fourier neural operator to learn the solution operator of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on tori with varying aspect ratios.
motivation: To develop a geometry-conditioned machine learning model that captures the distinct high-frequency cascade behaviors of the NLS equation on rational vs. irrational tori.
method: A Fourier neural operator is conditioned on the aspect ratio parameter and trained on data from Fourier pseudospectral simulations to approximate the one-step time evolution.
result: The learned operator reproduces the Sobolev norm growth differences between rational and irrational tori, with geometry conditioning improving long-time accuracy.
conclusion: Geometry-aware neural operators can effectively learn spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive PDEs.

title: Equivalence Of Continuous-Time Markov Chains And Linear Dynamical Systems
authors: Mihir Vahanwala
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The purpose of this short note is to record that an analogue of the following result, which is known for discrete-time linear dynamical systems, also holds in the continuous-time setting. The dynamics of a [MATH]-state Markov chain is governed by that of a linear dynamical system of dimension at most [MATH]; conversely, a linear dynamical system of dimension [MATH] can be "embedded" into a Markov chain with [MATH] states.
tldr: This note proves an equivalence between continuous-time Markov chains and linear dynamical systems, extending a known discrete-time result.
motivation: To establish a formal correspondence between Markov chains and linear dynamical systems in continuous time, which may have implications for modeling and simulation.
method: The author provides a constructive proof showing that the dynamics of an n-state Markov chain can be represented by a linear dynamical system of dimension at most n, and conversely, any linear dynamical system of dimension n can be embedded into a Markov chain with n+1 states.
result: The equivalence holds in continuous time, analogous to the discrete-time case, with explicit bounds on the dimensions.
conclusion: The result is a theoretical equivalence that may be useful for transferring techniques between Markov chains and linear systems, but it does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Self-Verifying Measurement Records: Hash-Linked Evidence Graphs For Hardware Benchmarking
authors: Baris Basaran Faruk Alpay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Performance numbers reported for hardware are accepted on trust: the reader cannot recompute them, the apparatus is gone, and the silicon itself can be silently wrong, with fleet studies reporting on the order of one core in a thousand returning incorrect arithmetic with no error raised. We make a reported hardware measurement a tamper-evident, independently checkable record. Every quantity in the text, a table, or a figure is bound, by its content hash, to the observation and the verification behind it; the whole is a hash-linked, append-only structure (a transparency log for measurement) that a verifier audits offline without trusting its producer. Matrix products are verified by a probabilistic identity (Freivalds) at O(k n^2) cost under a tolerance we derive from floating-point error analysis and calibrate to the device's own measured residual floor, so a wrong product is rejected with probability 1 - 2^(-k); quantities with no such identity carry an algebraic checksum and a measured reproducibility class. We then treat the check itself as a security object: a probe seed committed for offline reproducibility is an attack surface, and a probe-aware adversary can hide a corruption in the probe's null space, fooling even a quorum of bit-identical witnesses, while a Fiat-Shamir challenge derived from the claimed output closes this. Driving the device from an unprivileged tenant's reach, with a di/dt power virus and a thermal soak, neither moves the calibrated tolerance nor produces a silent error, placing the physical-fault threat at the rare defective part or the privileged attacker and marking the boundary at which the record must compose with a hardware root of trust. We demonstrate the construction across Blackwell and Hopper GPUs and report a residual-floor and reproducibility map by precision, size, and device.
tldr: A method to make hardware measurement records tamper-evident and independently verifiable using hash-linked evidence graphs.
motivation: Hardware performance numbers are often taken on trust, but devices can be faulty or malicious; the paper aims to provide a cryptographic guarantee of measurement integrity.
method: Each measurement is bound to its content hash, forming a hash-linked append-only log; matrix products are verified via Freivalds' probabilistic identity, and other quantities carry algebraic checksums and reproducibility classes.
result: The construction is demonstrated on Blackwell and Hopper GPUs, showing that power viruses and thermal stress do not produce silent errors, and the tolerance calibration is robust.
conclusion: The approach provides tamper-evident records that can be audited offline, but requires a hardware root of trust to defend against privileged attackers.

title: Which Nash Equilibrium? Solver-Dependent Selection On Zero-Sum Nash Polytopes
authors: Luis Leal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many two-player zero-sum games admit not a unique Nash equilibrium but a convex set of them: a polytope of profiles that all share the minimax value V* yet prescribe different behaviour. Standard solvers each converge to some equilibrium and are treated as interchangeable. We ask whether they instead select different members of the Nash set, systematically as a function of the algorithm rather than the seed. Using a tabular, exactly solvable testbed of six games with analytically known Nash sets -- including a two-dimensional Nash polytope and Kuhn poker -- we find that (i) selection is determined by the algorithm, not the seed, but families differ only on asymmetric Nash sets; (ii) regularized last-iterate methods (R-NaD, magnetic mirror descent) select the maximum-entropy member, the information projection of their uniform reference onto the Nash set -- exactly on the 2-D polytope and at 99.7% of maximum entropy in Kuhn -- while regret-averaging methods (CFR, CFR+, fictitious play) drift to a lower-entropy face; we confirm this on a randomized 180-game ensemble, where R-NaD attains the maximum-entropy member in 100% of converged games while CFR+ sits strictly below it in 94% (paired Wilcoxon p < 10^-27); (iii) the selected member has downstream consequences against sub-optimal opponents that scale with sequential/hidden-information structure but stay bounded -- in Kuhn the max-entropy member is a strictly better hedge, whereas on the matrix games the members differ without either dominating. We also report two negative results correcting common intuitions: removing CFR's positive-orthant (max(R,0)) projection does not eliminate boundary drift; and R-NaD's selection is anchor-following, not initialization-independent. We state the maximum-entropy / I-projection characterization as a strongly data-supported conjecture, checked throughout against analytic ground truth.
tldr: This paper studies how different Nash equilibrium solvers select among multiple equilibria in zero-sum games, focusing on the maximum-entropy selection property of regularized methods.
motivation: Standard solvers for zero-sum games are often treated as interchangeable, but they may systematically select different Nash equilibria from the convex set, which could affect downstream behavior against suboptimal opponents.
method: The authors use a tabular testbed of six games with analytically known Nash polytopes, including Kuhn poker, and compare solvers such as R-NaD, magnetic mirror descent, CFR, CFR+, and fictitious play. They also run a randomized 180-game ensemble for statistical validation.
result: Regularized last-iterate methods (R-NaD, magnetic mirror descent) select the maximum-entropy member of the Nash set, while regret-averaging methods (CFR, CFR+, fictitious play) converge to lower-entropy faces. The selection is algorithm-dependent, not seed-dependent, and has bounded downstream consequences.
conclusion: The maximum-entropy / I-projection characterization is strongly supported as a conjecture for regularized solvers, and the choice of solver matters for the specific equilibrium selected, especially in games with asymmetric Nash sets.

title: Observers, Symmetries, And The Hierarchy Of Language Classes: A Theory Of Computation Parameterized By The Observer
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27407v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce the , a new axis of classification for formal languages, orthogonal to the Chomsky hierarchy. An observer is a function [MATH] that determines which information about the input is accessible to a computational system. The order-blind automaton, which perceives the input as a multiset of symbols rather than a sequence, constitutes the paradigmatic case. We prove that the class of languages recognisable by any machine equipped with such an observer coincides exactly with the permutation-closed languages. We then define a partial order on observers that induces a hierarchy of language classes parametrised not by the computational power of the machine, but by the structure of the observer. We prove that this hierarchy has the structure of a partial order with a diamond-shaped profile sub-lattice, comprising the length branch [MATH] and the parity branch [MATH], with [MATH] and [MATH] incomparable, and an infinite subsequence branch [MATH], both converging to the complete observer. We prove that the observational hierarchy is strictly incomparable with the Chomsky hierarchy, and introduce the notion of of a language. We further define observer-parametrised complexity classes [MATH] and [MATH], and show that computational hardness and structural blindness are two independent phenomena. In particular, [MATH] holds as a structural collapse strictly inside [MATH].
tldr: The paper introduces a new classification axis for formal languages based on an 'observer' function, orthogonal to the Chomsky hierarchy, and defines observer-parametrized complexity classes.
motivation: To explore how the information accessible to a computational system (the observer) affects language recognition and complexity, independent of the machine's computational power.
method: Defines observers as functions that filter input information, studies automata with such observers (e.g., order-blind automata), and proves structural properties of the resulting language hierarchy.
result: The observer hierarchy is a partial order with a diamond-shaped sub-lattice, strictly incomparable with the Chomsky hierarchy; observer-parametrized complexity classes P_obs and NP_obs are introduced.
conclusion: Computational hardness and structural blindness are independent phenomena; the observer framework provides a new perspective on language classification.

title: Estimation--Prediction Tradeoff In Causal Probabilistic Temporal Graphs
authors: Aniq Ur Rahman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporal link prediction is usually evaluated by predictive performance on unseen edges, but in probabilistic temporal graphs this criterion can conflate model error with irreducible uncertainty. We study this issue by characterising an inherent estimation--prediction tradeoff in binary logistic models where regimes that maximise Fisher information and improve parameter recoverability are also those with the highest entropy, making individual predictions intrinsically harder even under perfect parameter recovery. We propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with transient edges and known ground-truth causal structure, allowing temporal link prediction to be evaluated jointly with causal parameter recovery. For the proposed binary logistic parametrisation, we derive the Cram\'{e}r--Rao bound and validate the tradeoff between parameter estimation error and irreducible predictive loss. Our results show that predictive accuracy alone may not reflect whether a model has learned the underlying causal mechanism, motivating benchmarks that distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty.
tldr: The paper studies an estimation-prediction tradeoff in causal probabilistic temporal graphs, focusing on binary logistic models and Fisher information.
motivation: Temporal link prediction often conflates model error with irreducible uncertainty; the authors aim to disentangle these by analyzing parameter estimation and predictive loss.
method: They propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with known ground-truth causal structure and derive the Cramér-Rao bound for binary logistic parametrization.
result: They show that regimes maximizing Fisher information also have highest entropy, making predictions harder even with perfect parameter recovery, validating a tradeoff between estimation error and predictive loss.
conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone may not reflect learning of causal mechanisms; benchmarks should distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic uncertainty.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper reviews the theory of Wannier functions and describes the interoperable software ecosystem, including codes for maximally localized Wannier functions and their applications.
result: The review catalogs the capabilities and interconnections of various software packages in the Wannier-function ecosystem.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling accurate and insightful materials simulations.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression due to oxide coverage.
motivation: To understand the microscopic electrostatic landscape in graphene devices with metal-oxide layers, which is crucial for optimizing electronic and spintronic performance.
method: In operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution is used to image the valence band edge across the device under bias and gate voltage, extracting a spectroscopic screening factor.
result: The electric field in graphene covered with oxides is suppressed by up to 50% compared to bare graphene, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to uncover potential landscapes in 2D devices, enabling advanced device engineering.

conclusion: Electric chirality control in helimagnets is feasible, offering a new pathway for spintronic devices.

title: Non-dipole Effects In Two-photon Double Ionization Of The K-shell Of A Beryllium-like Atomic Ion
authors: Alexey N. Hopersky, Alexey M. Nadolinsky, Rustam V. Koneev, Julia N. Kolesnikova
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the second order of the non-relativistic quantum perturbation theory and outside the framework of the dipole approximation for the operator of the radiation transition between continuum-spectrum states, the analytical structures and absolute values of the generalized cross-sections of the two-photon double ionization of the K-shell of beryllium-like ions of titanium (Ti18+), iron (Fe22+) and zinc (Zn26+) atoms were predicted. It has been established that taking into account non-dipole effects by several orders of magnitude (giant non-dipole effect) reduces the generalized cross-sections calculated within the framework of the dipole approximation. It has also been established that at high (12.5 - 28 keV) energies of the absorbed photons, the generalized cross-section of the two-photon double ionization of the K-shell is several orders of magnitude greater than the generalized cross-section of the single ionization. At the same time, as was to be expected, the transition from a neon-like ion to a beryllium-like ion is accompanied by a significant increase in the role of non-dipole effects.
tldr: The paper studies non-dipole effects in two-photon double ionization of beryllium-like ions, a topic in atomic physics.
motivation: To understand the role of non-dipole contributions in multi-photon ionization processes for highly charged ions.
method: Non-relativistic quantum perturbation theory beyond the dipole approximation for radiation transitions.
result: Non-dipole effects reduce generalized cross-sections by orders of magnitude; at high photon energies, two-photon double ionization dominates over single ionization.
conclusion: Non-dipole effects are significant and must be included for accurate cross-section predictions in such systems.

title: Toward A Hybrid Digital Twin Of Society: Quantifying Cognitive-Spatial Linkages Through Online-Offline Feedback Networks
authors: Julia Koltai Rafiazka Hilman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital platforms increasingly shape how people experience and navigate cities, linking virtual information seeking with physical mobility. Despite this interdependence, online and offline activities are often studied separately in urban mobility research. This paper introduces the Feedback Network, a computational framework that captures interactions between cognitive activity in digital environments and behavior in physical space. Using Google Search and Location History data from the same individuals, collected through a data donation framework in Budapest, Hungary, between 2018 and 2022, we examine how online search patterns and offline visitation behavior co-evolve. We combine semantic and spatial analytical approaches. Radius of gyration is adapted to measure variation in geographic mobility and semantic exploration, enabling comparison between physical movement and online cognitive dispersion. A Feedback Network models transitions between search-related and location-related activity clusters and is evaluated using Concentration Entropy, which measures whether behavioral flows are concentrated around routine pathways or distributed across exploratory transitions. The results show that online exploration is more concentrated than offline mobility, suggesting narrower and more repetitive semantic interests, while physical movement remains relatively diverse. Persistent linkages between search and visitation activities related to retail and business services indicate stable cognitive-spatial behavioral loops. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted spatial routines more strongly than cognitive exploration, widening the gap between digital engagement and realized movement. The findings demonstrate that urban mobility depends on the interaction between informational exposure and spatial encounter and provide a foundation for Hybrid Digital Twins of Society.
tldr: This paper studies the interplay between online search behavior and physical mobility in urban environments using a feedback network model.
motivation: Understanding how digital information seeking and physical movement co-evolve is important for urban planning and digital twin development.
method: The authors use Google Search and Location History data from individuals in Budapest, apply radius of gyration to measure mobility and semantic exploration, and model transitions with a Feedback Network evaluated by Concentration Entropy.
result: Online exploration is more concentrated than offline mobility; persistent cognitive-spatial loops exist for retail and business services; COVID-19 disrupted spatial routines more than cognitive exploration.
conclusion: Urban mobility depends on the interaction between informational exposure and spatial encounter, supporting the concept of Hybrid Digital Twins of Society.

title: Mosaic: A Benchmark Suite For Differentiable Physics Solvers
authors: Andrin Rehmann, Heiko Zimmermann, Dion H\"afner
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differentiable partial differential equation (PDE) solvers underpin solver-in-the-loop ML training, gradient-based optimal control, and inverse problems, yet the practical cost of obtaining correct, usable gradients from a given solver on a given problem is largely undocumented. Integration effort, computational cost, gradient accuracy, and numerical conditioning vary widely across solvers and are discoverable only by trial and error. We introduce Mosaic, an extensible benchmarking framework for differentiable PDE solvers that standardizes access to solver gradients. Each solver is packaged as a containerized component (Tesseract) exposing a uniform gradient API regardless of language or automatic differentiation (AD) strategy, enabling researchers to evaluate, compare, and build on non-trivial physical solvers. Our evaluation of 14 solvers across fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and heat transfer demonstrates that the benchmark surfaces practically relevant differences: order-of-magnitude variation in computational cost and Jacobian conditioning, alongside structural incompatibilities that eliminate solvers from realistic tasks entirely. Despite this variation, all solvers that produce gradients converge to similar optima, indicating that the practical barriers are memory limits, numerical stability, and setup compatibility rather than gradient accuracy alone. Mosaic is open-source and available at [URL].
tldr: Mosaic is a benchmark suite for differentiable PDE solvers, evaluating their gradients across fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and heat transfer.
motivation: The practical cost of obtaining correct, usable gradients from differentiable PDE solvers is undocumented, hindering solver-in-the-loop ML training and inverse problems.
method: The authors package each solver as a containerized component (Tesseract) with a uniform gradient API, and evaluate 14 solvers on computational cost, gradient accuracy, and numerical conditioning.
result: Order-of-magnitude variation in cost and conditioning is observed, but all solvers that produce gradients converge to similar optima, indicating memory limits and stability are the main barriers.
conclusion: Mosaic provides a standardized framework to compare differentiable PDE solvers, highlighting practical barriers beyond gradient accuracy.

title: Unidirectional Guided Resonances Enabled By Competing Fourier Harmonics Near The Fourth Stop Band
authors: Wook-Jae Lee Sun-Goo Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unidirectional guided resonances (UGRs) have attracted considerable attention owing to their remarkable ability to radiate exclusively in one direction from single-layer planar photonic lattices without metallic components. Conventionally, UGRs have been understood to require either broken in-plane [MATH] symmetry or interband coupling between distinct modes. Here, a new mechanism for realizing UGRs is presented, in which out-of-plane radiation near the fourth stop band is mediated by two distinct channels associated with the first and second Fourier harmonics. When the radiation components from the first and second Fourier harmonics cancel each other out in both the upward and downward directions, nonradiative bound states in the continuum emerge. By contrast, UGRs arise when such cancellation occurs only in one direction. By tuning the lattice parameters, the positions of these UGRs can be controlled, allowing them to merge at the [MATH] point. The two-channel radiation-cancellation model enables UGRs without relying on in-plane symmetry breaking or interband coupling, thereby relaxing lithographic constraints and simplifying device design. It also provides a useful framework for controlling topological singular states in higher-order photonic bands.
tldr: This paper presents a new mechanism for unidirectional guided resonances in photonic lattices using competing Fourier harmonics near the fourth stop band.
motivation: Unidirectional guided resonances are important for photonic devices, but conventional mechanisms require symmetry breaking or interband coupling, which complicate fabrication.
method: The authors propose a two-channel radiation-cancellation model where out-of-plane radiation from first and second Fourier harmonics cancel in one direction, enabling UGRs without symmetry breaking.
result: UGRs are realized by tuning lattice parameters to achieve cancellation in only one direction, and they can merge at the Γ point.
conclusion: This mechanism relaxes lithographic constraints and simplifies device design, offering a framework for controlling topological singular states in higher-order photonic bands.

title: Linking The "inner" And "outer" Self To Mental Health And Brain Networks
authors: Cosimo Agostinelli, Ivan Casanovas, Lochan Chaudhari, Arda Ergin, Pablo Est\'evez-Guti\'errez, Akanksha Gupta, Juliane T. Moraes, Mario Edoardo Pandolfo, Carlos Gershenson, Haily Merritt, Andreia Sofia Teixeira
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How are psychosocial profiles, mental health, and brain functional connectivity related? Studies have been dedicated to unraveling the associations of social support perception and neural functional connectivity. Additionally, personality traits have been explored by examining brain networks. Research on mental health has been developed using a broad range of methods and different approaches. However, little attention has been devoted to understanding how personality traits and social variables are related, and to what extent these components are reflected in brain functional connectivity and mental health outcomes. In this work, we aim to address these complex relations by using data from the Human Connectome Project, both from surveys and resting-state fMRI. The survey data includes personality traits measures and self-reported social support-related variables, which we will refer to as inner- and outer-self, respectively. It also includes data on mental health outcomes. Using z-score standardized measures, we analyze correlation matrices to evaluate the association between the inner- and outer-self domains. Our results show that the social indicators are more evidently grouped by impact on social experience than by the duality of inner-outer selves. Using a [MATH]-means clustering algorithm, we separate individuals into two groups according to social profiles. When confronting these results with the mental health outcomes, we show that the more socially desirable cluster exhibited a higher score on positive aspects such as life satisfaction and purpose in life. In the functional brain connectivity, we observe that the cluster with a more socially beneficial profile exhibits lower interconnectivity, especially in the default mode network. The pipeline we present uses a combined analysis of both fMRI and psychosocial variables, which could open the path for more extensive analysis.
tldr: This paper studies the relationship between psychosocial profiles, mental health, and brain functional connectivity using survey data and resting-state fMRI from the Human Connectome Project.
motivation: To understand how personality traits (inner self) and social support (outer self) are related and how they reflect in brain networks and mental health outcomes.
method: Correlation analysis of z-score standardized survey measures and k-means clustering to group individuals by social profiles, followed by comparison of mental health outcomes and functional brain connectivity between clusters.
result: Social indicators group more by impact on social experience than by inner/outer self; the socially desirable cluster shows higher life satisfaction and lower default mode network interconnectivity.
conclusion: The combined analysis of fMRI and psychosocial variables can reveal links between social profiles, mental health, and brain connectivity, opening avenues for further research.

title: On The Stability Of Scale-space Metrics
authors: William Leeb
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the stability of a classical family of metrics defined over functions' Gaussian scale-space representations, focusing on the comparison of images (functions of two variables). These metrics have precedents both in harmonic analysis, specifically the theory of Besov spaces, and in classical methods of image processing; special cases are also known to be metrically equivalent to certain Wasserstein distances. We quantify these metrics' robustness to geometric deformations, and introduce rotationally-invariant versions that are stable to changes in angle when comparing tomographic projections. We also describe computationally efficient algorithms for evaluating the metrics from finite samples, and prove their robustness to additive noise. The results are illustrated through numerical experiments.
tldr: This paper studies the stability of scale-space metrics for image comparison, with connections to Besov spaces and Wasserstein distances.
motivation: To quantify robustness of image metrics to geometric deformations and noise, and to develop rotationally-invariant versions for tomographic projections.
method: Theoretical analysis of metric stability under deformations and noise, plus computational algorithms for finite-sample evaluation.
result: Proved stability bounds and introduced rotationally-invariant metrics; demonstrated robustness numerically.
conclusion: Scale-space metrics are stable and computationally feasible for image comparison tasks.

title: Geometry-Preserving Reduced-Order Modeling Via Immersed Tensor Decomposition (itd)
authors: Lei Zhang, Jiachen Guo, Guowei He, Thomas J. R. Hughes, Wing Kam Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Body-fitted finite-element methods deliver high-order accuracy but hinge on a clean, watertight, conforming mesh, a requirement that breaks down for the geometrically imperfect CAD assemblies, image-based volumetric data, and voxel-native designs that pervade biomedical engineering and additive manufacturing, where mesh generation has become the dominant cost of the analysis cycle. Immersed methods on regular background Cartesian grids sidestep body-fitted meshing, but classical implementations integrate over irregular cut subdomains, destroying the tensor-product structure that enables separable, reduced-order methods such as tensor decomposition. In this paper we propose the (ITD) framework, which couples a mesh-free geometric representation via body-fitted function with the separable C-HiDeNN-TD reduced-order solver to enable large-scale simulation directly on regular background voxel meshes. The geometry is encoded in three steps: a signed-distance function represents the boundary, a body-fitted function [MATH] approximates it with controllable error, and a low-rank Tucker decomposition provides model-order reduction; for a fixed grid spacing [MATH], accuracy is improved by raising the approximation order of C-HiDeNN interpolation up to degree [MATH] with a linear background mesh. The central contribution is an exact Dirichlet formulation that enforces the boundary condition strongly by multiplying the trial function with [MATH], so that [MATH] holds by construction without any variational penalty or interface quadrature. We establish an a priori error estimate for the formulation and assess it on canonical 2D/3D domains, demonstrating optimal convergence and robustness on non-Cartesian geometries discretized by regular voxel meshes.
tldr: A reduced-order modeling framework for immersed finite-element methods on regular Cartesian grids, using tensor decomposition and body-fitted functions to handle complex geometries without conforming meshes.
motivation: Body-fitted meshing is a bottleneck for complex geometries from CAD, imaging, and additive manufacturing; immersed methods on Cartesian grids avoid meshing but lose tensor-product structure needed for efficient reduced-order models.
method: The ITD framework combines a signed-distance function for geometry, a body-fitted function for approximation, and low-rank Tucker decomposition for model-order reduction, with an exact Dirichlet formulation that enforces boundary conditions strongly via multiplication.
result: A priori error estimates are established, and numerical tests on 2D/3D domains show optimal convergence and robustness on non-Cartesian geometries discretized by regular voxel meshes.
conclusion: The ITD framework enables large-scale simulation directly on regular background voxel meshes without body-fitted meshing, preserving accuracy and tensor-product efficiency.

title: Analysis, Thermodynamics, And A Numeric Solver For A Pressure-temperature Equilibrium Closure Of The Four-equation Model
authors: Bennett Clayton, Joshua Mcconnell, Clell Solomon
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze an often used closure model for multi-material hydrodynamics where pressure temperature equilibrium (PTE) is assumed for every state; emphasis is placed on tabular equations of state. This multi-material model is often referred to as the four-equation model. The identification of the admissible set is presented and is proven to be convex, setting the foundation for development of invariant-domain methods for this model. A novel, robust, and efficient method is presented for solving the highly nonlinear system for the equilibrated pressure and temperature with an arbitrary number of materials. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the thermodynamics of the mixture model for general equations of state and prove existence and uniqueness of the pressure-temperature equilibrium solution under some thermodynamic assumptions.
tldr: This paper analyzes a pressure-temperature equilibrium closure for multi-material hydrodynamics, focusing on numerical methods and thermodynamic existence proofs.
motivation: To provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for the four-equation model used in multi-material hydrodynamics, ensuring robust numerical methods.
method: The authors identify the admissible set, prove its convexity, and develop a novel solver for the nonlinear pressure-temperature equilibrium system with tabular equations of state.
result: Existence and uniqueness of the pressure-temperature equilibrium solution are proven under thermodynamic assumptions, and a robust solver is presented.
conclusion: The work establishes a theoretical basis for invariant-domain methods in multi-material hydrodynamics, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics of computation, or quantum systems.

title: Zonal Spherical Functions Of Quantum Symmetric Pairs
authors: Philip Schl\"osser
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We identify the zonal and character spherical functions for quantum symmetric pairs with the symmetric Koornwinder--Macdonald polynomials. To this end, the methods of Letzter's 2004 paper are translated to modern conventions and right coideal subalgebras, and extended to non-standard cases and cases with non-reduced restricted root systems. For the last elusive Satake type, FII, a conjecture is provided.
tldr: The paper identifies zonal spherical functions for quantum symmetric pairs with symmetric Koornwinder–Macdonald polynomials, extending Letzter's methods to non-standard cases.
motivation: To understand the representation theory of quantum symmetric pairs and connect it to special functions.
method: Translates Letzter's 2004 methods to modern conventions and right coideal subalgebras, extending to non-standard and non-reduced root systems.
result: Zonal and character spherical functions are identified with symmetric Koornwinder–Macdonald polynomials, with a conjecture for the FII Satake type.
conclusion: The work provides a unified framework for spherical functions in quantum symmetric spaces, linking to known orthogonal polynomials.

title: Computing Accurate Singular Vectors And Eigenvectors Using Mixed-precision Jacobi Algorithms
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Fran\c{c}oise Tisseur, Marcus Webb
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed-precision variants of the Jacobi algorithm for symmetric positive definite eigenproblems and the one-sided Jacobi algorithm for singular value decompositions have recently been shown to compute eigenvalues and singular values to high relative accuracy. However, these analyses do not address the accuracy of the computed eigenvectors and singular vectors. In this paper, we prove error bounds for the computed eigenvectors and singular vectors, where the error is measured by the sine of the angle between the vector and its computed counterpart. The obtained bounds preserve the relative gap structure of the bounds for Jacobi algorithms proved by Demmel and Veseli\'{c}, but involve the scaled condition number of the preconditioned matrix rather than that of the original matrix (the former of which is typically much smaller). Numerical experiments support our theoretical bounds and demonstrate that the mixed-precision preconditioned Jacobi algorithms are especially effective for ill-conditioned matrices with small absolute gaps and moderate relative gaps between eigenvalues or singular values.
tldr: This paper proves error bounds for eigenvectors and singular vectors computed by mixed-precision Jacobi algorithms, focusing on numerical linear algebra rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Previous work showed mixed-precision Jacobi algorithms compute eigenvalues and singular values accurately, but accuracy of eigenvectors and singular vectors was unaddressed.
method: The authors derive error bounds measured by the sine of the angle between computed and true vectors, using the scaled condition number of the preconditioned matrix.
result: The bounds preserve the relative gap structure from Demmel and Veselić but involve a smaller condition number, and numerical experiments confirm effectiveness for ill-conditioned matrices.
conclusion: Mixed-precision preconditioned Jacobi algorithms compute eigenvectors and singular vectors accurately, especially for matrices with small absolute gaps and moderate relative gaps.

title: Reservoir Zero-Coordinatewise Projected Subspace Search For Minimization Over Sparse Symmetric Sets In Machine Learning
authors: Morteza Kimiaei, Shima Shabani, Michael Breuss
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a class of nonconvex cardinality-constrained optimization problems arising in sparse learning. These problems are NP-hard due to the combinatorial nature of sparsity constraints. We introduce a Reservoir Zero-Coordinatewise Projected Subspace Search (RZCW-PSS) algorithm, a simplex-style method on sparse manifolds that integrates coordinatewise search, symmetry-aware swap-based support updates, randomized low-dimensional subspace exploration, and zero-coordinatewise reservoir injection. The proposed method augments classical coordinate and swap moves with sparse-compatible subspace searches constructed from a dynamically maintained reservoir of previously accepted feasible points. A key feature of the approach is a refined reservoir initialization strategy that embeds sparse projection directly into a uniform sampling procedure, preserving geometric diversity within the feasible set. The algorithm also includes an optional support-identification safeguard that enforces full-support stabilization under a fixed support-change decrease threshold. We establish that, under the stated regularity, sampling, and subproblem-accuracy assumptions, every full-support accumulation point of the RZCW-PSS iterates is Beck--Hallak zero-coordinatewise stationary almost surely; with the safeguard and full-support initialization, this conclusion applies to all accumulation points. We further prove a conditional local linear convergence rate after support stabilization and derive the corresponding logarithmic local iteration complexity. Numerical experiments on synthetic sparse learning problems demonstrate that RZCW-PSS improves robustness and solution quality while remaining computationally competitive with Partial Simplex Search, Basic Feasible Search, and Zero-Coordinatewise Search methods.
tldr: This paper proposes a new algorithm for cardinality-constrained optimization in sparse learning, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Sparse learning problems are NP-hard due to combinatorial sparsity constraints, and existing methods may lack robustness or efficiency.
method: The Reservoir Zero-Coordinatewise Projected Subspace Search (RZCW-PSS) algorithm combines coordinatewise search, swap-based support updates, randomized subspace exploration, and a reservoir of feasible points.
result: The algorithm achieves zero-coordinatewise stationarity almost surely under regularity conditions and demonstrates improved robustness and solution quality on synthetic problems.
conclusion: RZCW-PSS is a competitive method for sparse optimization, but it is purely in the domain of machine learning and optimization, unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Commutative Topological Algebras On Translation-invariant Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
authors: Miguel Angel Rodriguez Rodriguez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study commutative topological algebras naturally associated with translation-invariant reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces whose direct integral decomposition has one-dimensional fibers. Starting from the bounded algebra of translation-invariant operators, we pass to a common dense domain generated by reproducing kernels and identify the corresponding diagonalizable operators with multiplication by symbols in an intersection of weighted [MATH]-spaces. On the symbol side this gives a canonical space [MATH] and a maximal multiplicative subalgebra [MATH], which is a complete locally convex [MATH]-algebra. Transporting the structure back yields corresponding algebras of operators and integral kernels. We also discuss when the inclusions [MATH] are strict, and illustrate the results with vertical and radial operators on classical Bergman and Fock spaces.
tldr: This paper studies commutative topological algebras on translation-invariant reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, focusing on operator algebras and symbol spaces.
motivation: To understand the algebraic structure of operators on certain function spaces and their diagonalization.
method: Uses direct integral decomposition and constructs dense domains from reproducing kernels to identify diagonalizable operators with multiplication operators.
result: Defines a canonical symbol space and a maximal multiplicative subalgebra, and discusses strictness of inclusions.
conclusion: Provides a framework for commutative algebras of operators on translation-invariant RKHS, with examples on Bergman and Fock spaces.

title: Second-Order Kkt Guarantees For Bregman Admm In Nonconvex And Non-Lipschitz Optimization
authors: Shuang Li, Zhihui Zhu, Qiuwei Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze Bregman ADMM for nonconvex linearly constrained problems under two-sided relative smoothness, a condition that replaces the standard Lipschitz gradient assumption with a Hessian comparison relative to a Bregman kernel. This setting covers polynomial objectives arising in matrix and tensor models for which a global Lipschitz-gradient constant need not exist. We show that on an invariant open state-space domain, one iteration of Bregman ADMM defines a smooth primal--dual fixed-point map whose strict-saddle KKT points are unstable fixed points; consequently, from random initialization the iterates converge to a strict saddle with probability zero. Combined with existing first-order convergence results, this yields almost-sure second-order stationarity of limiting KKT points. We extend the analysis to a multi-block star consensus formulation for distributed optimization. The technical novelty lies in a determinant reduction with a Bregman-specific symmetrization and scaling step in the two block spectral argument, together with a null space cancellation exploiting the star graph structure in the consensus case. Numerical experiments on distributed matrix factorization illustrate the theory, and a symmetric tensor factorization example demonstrates the broader Bregman proximal splitting idea beyond the separable consensus setting.
tldr: This paper provides second-order KKT guarantees for Bregman ADMM in nonconvex and non-Lipschitz optimization, focusing on matrix and tensor factorization.
motivation: Standard Lipschitz gradient assumptions fail for polynomial objectives in matrix/tensor models; the authors aim to prove convergence to second-order stationary points under weaker conditions.
method: They analyze Bregman ADMM under two-sided relative smoothness, using a determinant reduction with Bregman-specific symmetrization and a null space cancellation for star consensus.
result: They show that strict-saddle KKT points are unstable fixed points, so from random initialization iterates converge to a strict saddle with probability zero, ensuring almost-sure second-order stationarity.
conclusion: Bregman ADMM can guarantee second-order optimality for nonconvex problems without Lipschitz gradients, with applications to distributed matrix factorization and symmetric tensor factorization.

title: Tropical Fermat--Weber Problems Over Non-Finite Data And Their Inverse Formulations
authors: Ruriko Yoshida John Sabol
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The term tropical pseudonorm refers to a family of (not necessarily symmetric) gauge functions that arise in tropical or idempotent geometry. An important characteristic of these gauges is their invariance under translation by a constant vector, allowing them to descent naturally to tropical projective spaces. In this work, we explore the tropical one-infinity pseudonorm, a polyhedral hybrid gauge that allows for tunable asymmetry, in the context of a Fermat--Weber location problem. We extend previous formulations in considering non-finite data, and we investigate several variants of the inverse problem, providing linear programming formulations for their solution.
tldr: This paper studies tropical Fermat-Weber problems with non-finite data and their inverse formulations using linear programming.
motivation: To extend tropical location theory to handle data points at infinity and to solve inverse problems that recover parameters from given solutions.
method: The authors define the tropical one-infinity pseudonorm and formulate the Fermat-Weber problem as a linear program, then derive inverse variants also solvable via linear programming.
result: They provide linear programming formulations for both forward and inverse tropical Fermat-Weber problems with non-finite data.
conclusion: The work advances tropical geometry applications in location analysis but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Provable Reductions In Tfnp
authors: Noah Fleming, Stefan Grosser, Toniann Pitassi, Robert Robere
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new family of propositional proof systems, denoted , for an arbitrary TFNP search problem [MATH]. Informally, a refutation of a CNF formula [MATH] in is given by a polynomial-time reduction from the false-clause search problem [MATH] to [MATH], combined with an Extended Frege proof that the reduction is correct. These are motivated in two ways: 1. They are the propositional translations of witnessing theorems in bounded arithmetic, by which proofs of [MATH] formulas [MATH] in a theory [MATH] imply algorithms solving the search problem for [MATH] in a TFNP class corresponding to [MATH]. 2. They are a white-box analogue of the characterizations of proof systems using decision tree reductions to black-box TFNP problems. We consider the proof system , where Iter is a complete problem for PLS. We prove that is polynomially equivalent to the sequent calculus [MATH], and also to the implicit Resolution proof system [EF, Resolution]. Hence [MATH] and [EF, Resolution] are equivalent, which is the first characterization of an implicit proof system by a classical proof system beyond the work of Wang. We also consider for general TFNP relations [MATH]. We observe that if EF can prove that a search problem [MATH] is in FP, then is polynomially equivalent to EF. This contrasts to our above result, which shows that Extended-Frege provable reductions to [MATH], a problem widely believed not to be in FP, yields a proof system ([MATH]) that is believed to be stronger than Extended Frege. Finally, we show that for any proof system [MATH] which is sufficiently strong, there is a polynomial-time computable search problem [MATH] FP such that is polynomially equivalent to [MATH]. Letting [MATH] [EF, Resolution] and combining our two results shows that is polynomially equivalent to .
tldr: This paper introduces a new family of propositional proof systems based on TFNP search problems and studies their equivalence to classical proof systems.
motivation: To connect TFNP search problems with propositional proof complexity and to characterize implicit proof systems via classical ones.
method: Defines proof systems where refutations are polynomial-time reductions from false-clause search to a TFNP problem, combined with Extended Frege proofs of correctness; analyzes equivalences with sequent calculus and implicit Resolution.
result: Proves that the proof system based on the PLS-complete problem Iter is polynomially equivalent to the sequent calculus G and to implicit Resolution, and shows general equivalences for other TFNP problems.
conclusion: The work provides new connections between TFNP, bounded arithmetic, and proof complexity, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: What Was That Again? Certified Robustness For Automatic Speech Recognition
authors: Andrew C. Cullen, Neil Marchant, Jiani Xie, Paul Montague, Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition systems are notoriously both sensitive to adversarial and benign perturbations. While this has been repeatedly demonstrated using reference datasets, detecting such behaviors in deployed systems is incredibly challenging, due to the absence of oracle knowledge of the true transcription. We demonstrate that employing a certification-inspired mechanism can significantly decrease WER, increase recall, and decrease the Spearman correlation between confidence and WER. We achieve this through a dual-gate diagnostic pipeline: a Two-Sided Atomic Audit that accumulates statistical wealth to certify both token existence and adversarial exclusion, and a Rank-Based Tournament that selects the winning sequence. Our evaluations across four diverse architectures demonstrate up to a 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate, while also providing granular word- and sentence-level certifications to enhance acoustic security.
tldr: This paper proposes a certification-inspired method to improve robustness of automatic speech recognition systems against adversarial and benign perturbations.
motivation: Automatic speech recognition systems are sensitive to perturbations, but detecting such behaviors in deployed systems is challenging due to lack of oracle knowledge of true transcription.
method: A dual-gate diagnostic pipeline consisting of a Two-Sided Atomic Audit for statistical certification and a Rank-Based Tournament for sequence selection.
result: Achieves up to 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate across four diverse architectures, with granular word- and sentence-level certifications.
conclusion: The proposed method enhances acoustic security and robustness of ASR systems without requiring oracle knowledge.

title: Co-Optimization Of Analog Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks For Low-Power Function Approximation In Flexible Electronics
authors: Paula Carolina Lozano Duarte, Georgios Zervakis, Mehdi Tahoori, Sani Nassif
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27892v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wearable devices and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors require on-sensor processing of biosignals and environmental data, including computationally demanding operations such as nonlinear activation functions for neural network inference, sensor calibration curves to map raw readings to physical units, and signal preprocessing functions like logarithmic compression and power operations for feature extraction. These functions exhibit significant complexity, often involving transcendental operations and multivariate dependencies that are costly to implement digitally. Analog function approximation provides a power-efficient alternative by performing these computations in the analog domain, thereby reducing the energy overhead associated with analog-to-digital conversion and subsequent digital processing. Flexible Electronics (FE) present a particularly attractive platform for wearable applications due to mechanical flexibility and low-cost fabrication, but impose strict constraints on circuit density and power consumption, making efficient analog implementations critical but challenging. This work introduces Analog Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (AKANs), developed via hardware-software co-optimization, to approximate these complex multivariate functions accurately under hardware imperfections. Our method incorporates circuit-level error modeling during training and applies pruning at both software and hardware levels to reduce area and power. Validation across multiple benchmarks demonstrates that our proposed pruning methodology not only reduces hardware cost but can also improve approximation accuracy by regularizing spline parameters. Results show up to 55% area and 50% power savings, with average reductions of nearly 30% across datasets, highlighting AKANs as a robust and generalizable framework for low-power analog function approximation in FE.
tldr: This paper presents a hardware-software co-optimization framework for analog Kolmogorov-Arnold networks to approximate complex functions in low-power flexible electronics.
motivation: Wearable and IoT devices require energy-efficient on-sensor processing of nonlinear functions, which are costly to implement digitally. Flexible electronics impose strict area and power constraints, motivating analog function approximation.
method: The authors propose Analog Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (AKANs) with circuit-level error modeling during training and pruning at both software and hardware levels to reduce area and power.
result: The method achieves up to 55% area and 50% power savings with average reductions of nearly 30% across benchmarks, and pruning can improve approximation accuracy by regularizing spline parameters.

title: Transversal Difference Numbers In Finite Abelian Quotients
authors: Mugurel Barcau, Vicen\c{t}iu Pa\c{s}ol, George C. \c{t}urca\c{s}
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27961v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given \(H\leq G\) finite abelian groups, a transversal \(T\subseteq G\) for \(G/H\) has fixed size \(|G/H|\), but its ambient difference support \(D(T)=T-T\) can vary with the embedding of \(H\) in \(G\). We call [MATH] the transversal difference number of the pair \((G,H)\). This invariant is related to finite abelian factorisation, tiling complements, and small-sumset questions, and is motivated by recent work regarding ambient Galois labels in CRT transforms for cyclotomic-subfield homomorphic encryption. We prove various results regarding this invariant, including a general lower bound [MATH] where \(m(G,H)\) is the largest order of a subgroup of \(G\) disjoint from \(H\). The bound is sharp for cyclic quotients, and Kneser's theorem gives a cross-transversal estimate leading to exact product families with one nonsplit cyclic coordinate and arbitrary split factors. These results isolate the first genuinely new residual obstruction, namely the same-prime square plane \[ G=(\mathbb Z/p^2\mathbb Z)^2,\qquad H=pG. \] For odd \(p\), this case is the technical core of the paper. Here transversals are graphs of functions \(\mathbb F_p^2\to \mathbb F_p^2\), and \(D(T)\) decomposes into carry-corrected finite-field derivative images. We conjecture that \[ \delta(G,H)=(2p-1)^2 \] for all odd primes \(p\), prove the unconditional lower bound \(3p^2-p-1\), and give small-prime, probabilistic, and fixed-polynomial evidence for the conjecture.
tldr: The paper studies transversal difference numbers in finite abelian groups, an invariant related to factorization and tiling, motivated by homomorphic encryption.
motivation: To understand how the difference set of a transversal varies with the embedding of a subgroup, with applications to CRT-based homomorphic encryption.
method: Uses combinatorial and group-theoretic arguments, including Kneser's theorem, to derive lower bounds and exact formulas for specific group pairs.
result: Proves a general lower bound involving the largest order of a subgroup disjoint from H, and gives exact results for product families; identifies a critical case (Z/p^2Z)^2 with H=pG and provides evidence for a conjectured value.
conclusion: The invariant isolates a new obstruction in abelian group factorization, with the square plane case being the technical core.

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article addresses the combinatorial complexity inherent in modern high-tech system design by presenting automation-in-design (AiD) as a transformative paradigm. We propose computational design synthesis (CDS), a framework utilising deep learning and generative AI to automate the creation of novel systems. Two case studies (e-drive system design and spatial dimensioning problem) serve as proof-points for this approach. The AI-driven methods used in the case studies represent a fundamental shift in engineering, advancing from simulation-based optimisation towards autonomous design with minimal human supervision.
tldr: This paper presents an AI-driven computational design synthesis framework for automating high-tech system design, with case studies in e-drive and spatial dimensioning.

conclusion: The approach represents a paradigm shift in engineering design, but the paper focuses on classical engineering automation rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
